speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DISTINGUISHED VISITOR-EMPEROR HAILE SELASSIE OF ETHIOPIA
speechtext:
This morning there occurs one of those very rare but indeed very happy occasions, when it is my privilege to draw the attention of the house to the presence in our gallery of a most distinguished visitor. I refer to His Imperial Majesty, Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia. I take it as a great honour to be able, in your name, to extend to him a most hearty welcome. If ever a man possessed the virtues of courage, perseverance and love of country, it is the Emperor of the ancient Kingdom of Ethiopia. We cannot but admire the statesman who, in the darkest hour, when the league of nations had unfortunately decided to recognize the conquest of Ethiopia, stoutly answered, "Whatever the world will do, my people will fight on until they have forced the invader from the country or are themselves exterminated."
From then on he worked hard and prepared himself for what was to come. He had refused to bow to brute force, and once more in the history of the world faith and honesty were to triumph. I need not recite all the events which took place but a few years ago, events which are well known by all of you. Yet, it may be useful to recall such great deeds for the benefit of those who will come after us.
It was on January 15, 1941, that Haile Selassie arrived in Ethiopia from his Sudan headquarters, and there unfurled his red, green and yellow banner, rallied around him some of his faithful warriors in a secret rendezvous, and inspired his subjects to raise their arms and join a gradually expanding army. A few months later he returned to the throne and in less than a year, with the help of the allies, his beloved country was again completely free and independent.
(Translation):
Having extended a most cordial welcome to His Majesty Haile Selassie I, Emperor of Ethiopia, to this parliament, in Ottawa, and recalled the virtues of faith and courage which have inspired his conduct in life, I would feel remiss in my duty were I not to associate my French-speaking colleagues in the tribute I have paid him on behalf of the members of this house.
(Text):
There is not much more to be said at this time, except perhaps to recall briefly that although geographically our countries may appear far distant, they are very close together in the way of understanding and fraternity. This becomes evident when we stop to think of the numerous Canadians now living in Ethiopia and helping to make of that great country a country greater still, of a deserving nation, a happy and prosperous nation.
To Your Majesty we express our thanks for coming to Canada, and our regret that your visit must be so short. When you leave us, you will carry with you, I assure you, the best wishes of the people of this country for you personally, and the members of your family, your parliament, and your valiant people.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, by way of a brief explanation, I should like to speak for a moment or two on the estimates which are now before the committee.
These estimates cover the operation of the customs and excise division of the Department of National Revenue, consisting of the headquarters at Ottawa and their operative branches, consisting of some 232 ports and 104 outports situated throughout the country. As the committee is aware, this division is closely associated with the industry and commerce of the country through its control of imported goods and the collection of customs duties, as well as excise and sales taxes, and of the excise duties on alcohol and tobacco products. There is also a more pleasant association, at least from the importers' point of view, through the procedures for the refunds and drawbacks of duties and taxes remitted under certain conditions.
In addition to this relationship with industry and commerce from which, by the way, we derive by far our greatest customs and excise revenue, this division is concerned with a phase of work which is more familiar to the general travelling public, that of examining persons, motor vehicles, aircraft, trains and ships entering Canada.
A third phase of the division's activity is supervision under the Excise Act of those licensed establishments who manufacture or use alcohol or tobacco in the manufacture of their products.
In keeping with the general development of the country, more goods were imported into Canada in the fiscal year ending the 31st of March, 1954, than ever before, there being over 60,000 more import entries than in the fiscal year 1953, which reached an alltime high of 3,365,695 import entries. Again more vehicles than ever before travelled back and forth across our boundaries. In the fiscal year ending 1954, over thirteen and a half million vehicles, carrying returning Canadians and Americans, entered Canada, which was over 900,000 more than the fiscal year ending March 1953. In the calendar year ending 31st December, 1953, there were over one million more vehicles entering Canada than in the previous calendar year.
You will see in the estimates an increase in the number of positions and in the amount for salaries. This is directly related, over and above the general increase in civil service salaries, to the increasing amount of work which this division is called upon to perform. I should like to tell the committee that the staffing of our ports is rigidly controlled on a systematic basis, whereby the department 83276-348
Supply-National Revenue can gauge very accurately the number of staff required at ports in relation to the amount of business which is presented to and processed through the port, the hours of service required for the general and importing public, and the number of points of duty which have to be manned by customs officials at international border points throughout Canada. I think the committee will agree with me that in this division, which is responsible for the collection of revenue, amounting to over $1,518 million in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, any arbitrary method of staff restriction which is not realistically geared to the actual facts could result in a loss of revenue, if by physical inability, inadequate customs and excise examination and supervision resulted.
The estimates as tabled before you show an increase of $2,643,131, but 95 per cent of this is accounted for by salaries and wages, the remainder being made up of such things as law and other costs, uniforms, telephone, telegraph, teletype costs, and so forth.
At the same time there is a decrease of $86,400 in vote 298, construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment over last year's estimates.
I shall be pleased to answer any questions from the committee concerning these estimates.

I have listened with interest to the recital by the minister of the mounting activity, accompanied of course by the mounting work, and I have also listened with interest to his explanation that the additional amount being expended is nearly all salary increases.
I was surprised that the minister said nothing about one aspect of the work which seemed to me important, and which I thought he would refer to because of the legislation which was passed in December last. I refer of course to the amendment of the Customs Act, which proposed to deal with dumping. I should like to recall to the minister one or two of the things which he said in December last. I should like to recall that he and others stressed that this was not a tariff measure, that it was a measure of law enforcement; and I wish that could be said loudly enough so that some people of the baser sort would not insist, as soon as anyone speaks about the enforcement of the tariff law, that he at once becomes a high-as-Haman's-gallows tariff man. It was made very clear in this debate on both sides of the house that what we were attempting was the enforcement of law. I propose to ask the minister to give us something in the nature of a progress report on the act and its effects, on the steps which have been

Supply-National Revenue taken to make it effective, and on the results.
I should like to remind the minister briefly of one or two things which he said in December last, as reported at page 674 of Hansard as follows:

He also said:

Everyone will agree that the progress of events since that time, the existence of substantial unemployment, the manifest difficulties which certain industries are finding, and in general the whole trend of business from a seller's to a buyer's market justifies us in asking the minister to explain in more detail what steps have been taken to make the enforcement satisfactory, and just what the results are.

With reference to the other matter brought up by the hon. member for Greenwood, this of course has reference to the change that was made in December last, in this session, in the Customs Act whereby the valuation for duty purposes was changed. Subsection 6 was added to section 35 of the act, which attempted to deal with a particular problem that presented itself at that time, and probably to a certain extent continues to come before us and will continue to come before us for some time. The amendment at that time was to this effect:
(6) Notwithstanding anything in this act, where the market price of any manufactured goods in the country of export-
I would draw the committee's attention particularly to that last sentence. It continues:
-has. as the result of the advance of the season or the marketing period, declined to levels that do not reflect in the opinion of the minister their normal price, the value for duty shall be the amount determined and declared by the minister

to be the average price, weighted as to quantity, at which the like or similar goods were sold for consumption in the country of export during a reasonable period, not exceeding six months, immediately preceding the date of shipment of the goods to Canada.
I think I should perhaps read the rest of the instructions which were given to our officers in an attempt to carry out this provision of the act:
To give effect to the purpose of this amendment, collectors, appraisers, and any officer acting as appraiser, are instructed to closely scrutinize the invoice values of all manufactured goods, comparing such values with home market values shown and certified on previous importations of similar goods by the same or other importer. In any case where invoice values indicate price decline, such as is contemplated by the foregoing valuation provision, or the values appear abnormally low, the importer is to be advised that the entry may be subject to amendment in accordance therewith. The invoice is to be forwarded to the department with as full information as possible and the reasons for believing that the value shown is below the normal value, in order that the matter may be inquired into and the value for duty established as provided for by the new subsection of section 35.
This instruction was also issued to our collectors:
For the purpose of administration of section 35(6) of the Customs Act, referred to on page 1-44 of the book of instructions to port officers-
We send out instructions to all port officers as to how they are to carry out the law.
-importers are to be instructed to advise their suppliers that customs invoices covering manufactured goods of the type contemplated by this section will require to show, in addition to the usual fair market value and selling price data, the highest price at which like or similar goods were sold and delivered for home consumption during the six months immediately preceding the date of shipment to Canada. Typical of the goods which might be affected by this section are style fabrics, dresses, textiles, shoes and purses; refrigerators; automobiles. This list is illustrative only and is by no means exhaustive; and officers should use their own judgment in determining whether other goods are affected at their individual ports.

Supply-National Revenue You understand the significance of that. It means that in the last instance the value for duty purposes per piece was $3.35 compared with $2.97. These figures indicate to me at least that the value of these invoices per piece went up to $3.35 from $2.97, a difference of 38 cents per piece. When an invoice comes in and, by reason of our investigations, it is changed from X dollars and a different value is put on it up to $3.35 and duty is paid on that, that certainly must be a deterrent to importers to bring end of the season and end of the line goods into this country, and our manufacturers would have the advantage of that increase in price.

I assure the hon. member and the minister that I have no desire whatever to introduce any heat or acrimony into this discussion of the estimates. I was under the impression that the questions that have been asked by the hon. member for Greenwood, and the points that have been put forward were entirely within the understanding that had been discussed, and the hon. member for Greenwood had referred to this question of tariff as a necessary protection to the interpretation that is sometimes placed on the discussion of this matter. I am raising something that has only been brought to my attention within the last few minutes which has to do with what appears to be a very serious situation developing in the automobile industry. I would point out that if there is some other place within these estimates where this should be discussed I am prepared to discuss it then.
I was under the impression, however, that the administration of this act is under the minister, and that if, for instance, there were to be an inquiry into the situation in the automobile industry similar to that which is to be conducted with respect to the textile industry, it would be appropriate to place that suggestion before the minister whose estimates are now before us. If I am incorrect in that, I am prepared to put it forward otherwise, but if the hon. member has had an opportunity to read the announcement that just came over the wire a short time ago he will know that the president of the Ford company has announced that, contrary to earlier expectations, a drop in production-

On a point of order, I wonder whether all hon. members will be permitted to take part in a discussion of the very serious unemployment situation that is developing. I am sure a number of members in this group would like to take part in such a discussion if it is in order.

Mr. Chairman, this is the house of parliament and it is the duty of parliament at the earliest appropriate moment to deal


with matters of importance. This is something that will very seriously affect not only Windsor and Oakville but all other communities supplying the various parts of these automobiles. It is an entirely unexpected development, and I submit it is the duty of parliament to place the facts before those who have a substantial measure of responsibility in this matter at the first opportunity. I will simply ask the minister if it is not so that it would be within his power to order an inquiry in relation to the application of the anti-dumping measures administered by his department similar to that which is to be conducted with respect to the textile industry.

Of course I think the Leader of the Opposition knows that it is not within my power to instigate any such investigation. To date there is no evidence that this condition of unemployment in Windsor and the releasing of a number of employees there has anything whatever to do with the importation of automobiles into Canada either whole or in parts. I heard the announcement over the radio, and apart from that I know nothing about it. My understanding is that the layoff is for a short period of time and it may be due to changes in design or patterns or some part of the establishment being held up. I think that it is probably due to lack of consumer buying. I have heard that there is a war on between the Ford people and General Motors and that they have large inventories of stocks. Therefore I would not be a bit surprised that probably as the result of increased inventories it has been necessary for them to take this step. But at this time I can assure the hon. member that it has nothing to do with dumping into this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister permit one question? Did he not hear the whole of the radio news item-
No, I did not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -which was to the effect that only a portion of the lay-off is temporary and a large portion is not.
I did not hear the whole thing.

The minister's figures of recent prices compared, I understand, with those of last December seem to indicate a rather satisfactory situation, that is to say, that from the point of view of the customs administration the prices for duty purposes are now somewhat higher. But I should like to get at this point. Could we get figures showing comparative prices some months earlier? Furthermore, and this is particularly what I want to get, how many reports have

been received in response to the two directives which were sent out? It seems to me that would give us an indication as to how large a situation there was requiring treatment.

I am unable to give the exact number of reports that have been received but it must have been very considerable because I have given the answer with respect to where action has been taken and I have given information as to the great number of cases that are under investigation at the present time. This does not mean that delivery of these goods is not made to the importer or buyer. We reserve the right to reconsider and reassess the amount of duty that shall be paid. That means that with respect to these items and commodities under investigation the final determination has not been made of the amount that shall be paid on the invoices because the invoices may be reappraised and corrected.
I am not asking the minister for an exact detailed figure but surely he can indicate to me whether they have received scores of reports or hundreds of reports. I merely want a rough figure.
All over the country it would run into hundreds of reports from the different ports.
So that you have the situation of hundreds of reports coming in indicating a situation which requires the consideration of the department under the terms of the act of last December.
That is right.
You have these cases under review now.
Yes.

Last December, when the matter was under debate in the house, the minister gave us a good deal of information as to how typical prices in the United States were arrived at. Was I correct in understanding then that the organization for finding those prices was going to be set up?
That is right. It has been.

Would the minister say a bit more about that? While I am on my feet, I have one other question. I think he spoke about four countries being involved. Am I correct? I thought I heard that somewhere in the minister's statement. Well, I abandon that and I would ask the minister to give me further information as to the method of organization to make the situation more shipshape and watertight.
Supply-National Revenue

I might indicate to the hon. member for Greenwood that since December we have taken on 26 additional appraisers. These people are delegated from here to examine into exporters' prices, and are operating from here in the United States.
Are these officials all in the United States?
No, not all in the United States at the one time.
Where else?

Some of them are in the
United Kingdom. We are communicating with some other people with a view to having appraisers accepted in their countries. You just cannot walk in, you know, and send an appraiser into a country that is exporting something into Canada, then have him investigate prices in the country of origin. There has to be negotiation with these countries, and as the need arises we do that. Presently, our people are in the United States and Great Britain principally because they are the biggest exporters to this *country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister indicated that investigations were being made-under the provisions of the statute that has been under discussion-into a number of lines. As I listened to the list, it seemed to consist mainly of textiles and clothing items, but he referred also to refrigerators. Could he say what kind of refrigerators he had in mind? Could he say whether any other items of household equipment, such as stoves, furnaces and so on are under investigation?
When he answers those questions, could he say something as to the effect on Canadian importers which might arise from the knowledge that duties on these imports could be increased several months after the goods have been brought into the country? There are those who suggest that this is having a deterring effect on the importation of such goods as household equipment.

In answer to the hon. member's question, I am informed that the type of refrigerators that have been imported are mostly household refrigerators. There have not been many other articles of household effects.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I mean are they electrical, ice or gas or all three?

It is hard to answer what particular type, whether they have been electric, ice or gas. They would all be subject to the dumping duty if they were end of the line or seasonal stuff that were being shipped into Canada. So far as the type goes, the

Supply-National Revenue list only indicates the different models. There are a lot of different models, and I presume the model means the size.
So far as the application of the dumping duty is concerned, the department administers it with due care and reason. So far we have had no complaints from the importers because of delay or because of the unfair application of this valuation for duty purposes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I suppose, however, the department would not know whether any importers were refraining from trying to import because of the fear of what would happen.
No, I emphasized that at the start. There is no one who can determine how many importers have been deterred from making importations by reason of the application of this section.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I realize that it is a point on which statistics would not be available. There are some of us who fear that that is what is happening. There is another subject, Mr. Chairman, I want to ask questions about, but if the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton has a question in the same field, I shall yield and come back to this later.
My question is related to the administration of this amendment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Go ahead.

I am not quite clear, and perhaps the minister could make it more plain, who instigates this action to increase this duty. Is it the department on its own initiative that gives instructions to the customs collectors at points of entry or does the department just act when a request is received from an industry? For instance, you raised the duty on these textile goods, and it went up from month to month. Who instigated that? Was it your customs men at the border who took action as the goods came through or was this done at the request of an industry? I should like that cleared up.

I am sure that if the hon. member is conversant with what has happened within the last few months he will know that public demand and governmental action brought about the amendment. This parliament passed it, and that was the start of it. We, as administrators, through our appraisers put into effect the application of the amendment. We did not instigate it, we applied it. Does that answer your question?

I am afraid I am not making myself clear. I readily understand that the act was amended as the result of the demands of industry generally. The point I have in mind is this. Suppose I go

to the United States and buy some article, such as a refrigerator, a radio or piece of household furniture. I bring it to the border. Is it the duty of the customs inspector, regardless of whether the article is listed on that list, to check the price and raise the invoice? Who is going to decide whether the invoice should be raised at the border?
That is what our appraisers are there for. That is what we are paying our good money to them for, to appraise these goods at the price-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is it good money?

It is the very best; none of this new stuff. Perhaps the hon. member was not here at the time I read the instructions giving effect to this amendment. Collectors, appraisers and any officers acting as appraisers are instructed to closely scrutinize the invoice value of all manufactured goods and compare such values with the home market values shown and certified by previous importations. They have a pattern there to follow. What would a refrigerator like this be invoiced at a month ago? They can look that up. Why would this one be invoiced at $25 less, even if you brought it to the border yourself. We compare it and put up the valuation, and you pay the duty on that increased value.

I want to go a step farther now; that is not the end of it. Then these appraisers that you have are sent to the country of export to investigate and ascertain if this price that has been arbitrarily set at the border is fair and reasonable?

No. The point is this: Is the value at which they are exported the fair and reasonable value, comparable to the price at which they have been selling in their own country, under comparable conditions? But if at the end of a season they want to dump 10,000 manufactured articles into this country, or so many thousand yards of end of the season or end of the line, we say, "No, you cannot do that unless you invoice them at a value based on the weighted index of what you have been selling them for in your own country for the last six months, prior to this export".
How does the collector at the border know that these goods I am bringing in are end of the line goods?

He does not know. But here is the further instruction:
The invoice is to be forwarded to the department with as full information as possible of the reasons for believing that the value shown is below the normal value in order that the matter may be inquired into and the value for duty established, as provided by the new sub-section (6) of section 35.
I thank the minister for being patient with me. But in those instructions I heard him read there is no mention of end of the season.
You have to read the instructions in conjunction with the section of the act.
The minister has referred to differentials in prices for the various months of 1953 and 1954. Those prices, I presume, are the appraised prices for duty purposes, are they?
These are the declared prices on their invoices, by the importer.
These are the invoiced prices, not the appraised prices?
No, not the appraised prices; they are the declared prices.
Could the minister give us an indication in respect of the piece goods to which he has referred as to the final appraised price for duty purposes placed on these particular items by his department?
I do not know that we can give that information to the hon. member, because we must always be careful not to disclose the business of individuals or firms to the public.

The minister has indicated that the invoiced prices on a particular item is a certain amount. Is he giving away any more information there than he would be giving away if he gave us the price for that same item established by his department for duty purposes? In other words, how big a spread is there between the invoiced price and the appraised price for duty purposes?

It would vary from item to item. But the indication I have given is that in April a year ago, let us say, the price was $2.97 and now it is $3.35. So that you have that invoice jacked up to the extent of 38 cents per piece. And the percentage of that would be about 10 per cent above the price at which similar goods would have been invoiced, and were invoiced, in April a year ago.

We have a spread here from $2.97 to $3.35. That $3.35 price which the minister mentioned a minute ago was the invoiced price. In other words, the invoiced price, the actual cost of the goods in the country of origin, has increased in the last year; is that correct?

That is correct.
Supply-National Revenue
On this particular item the invoice now is $3.35. What is the appraised price for duty purposes placed on that particular item?
This would be the appraised price, too, in this instance.
What would be the invoiced price, the actual cost of these goods in the country of origin?
That would not make much difference to us, because it would be on a percentage basis. We would compare the invoiced price with the actual average price for six months in the home market.

From the minister's own statement the cost of these particular items, these piece goods, has gone up in the last year. Yet, presumably, a higher rate of duty is being applied against them through the application of this anti-dumping legislation. I was perhaps under a misapprehension that the price had somehow taken a big slide or slump in the last year, and that the goods were being dumped into Canada at prices considerably below the prices charged for the same items a year ago. Yet, according to the minister's statement, we have the invoiced price substantially increased, and now subject to a still higher rate of duty, through the application of the anti-dumping provision.

The whole point I attempted to make in giving these figures was that the legislation of December has had some effect in bringing the price up to a level that would represent a fair market value of the goods in question, as against the dumping price. So we have a price of $3.35 as against what you might call the dumping price of $2.97.

I can come to only one conclusion from that, sir, and that is that the price quoted at $3.35 for this item is not the invoiced price of that item in the country of origin but is, rather, the appraised price which the minister's department has placed upon it. In other words, it is the appraised price for duty purposes, and is not the invoiced price.
It could be the invoiced price accepted by us, and then would be also the appraised price.

The minister says it could be. May I ask if we can have submitted or read to us, or placed on the record in some way, a comparative statement covering, let us say, the first four months of 1953 and the first four months of the current year. That would be a comparative statement for all the items

Supply-National Revenue where there has been a difference between the invoiced price of the manufactured article and the appraised price for duty purposes? In other words it would include all items where the anti-dumping ruling has been applied.
In that comparative statement could we have a breakdown of the type of item, the volume brought into Canada, and then the following information: The appraised price, by items and by total value each month for each item; the appraised price for duty purposes per unit and per total value for each item; and, finally, a statement for each item for each month showing the total increase in duty imposed on all those items upon which anti-dumping legislation has been applied?

Mr. Chairman, that would be a monumental task. Before I would attempt it I would have to revise these estimates and ask for an extra appropriation to carry out the work-because an enormous amount of work would be involved. If there is any particular item that the hon. member is interested in, about which he wants information, we shall try to get it from the department for him. But such a general request as the hon. member has made, I am afraid, would cost an awful lot of time and money and would need a lot more employees in the department.

Mr. Chairman, actually what I am asking for would not involve a great deal of work. There are a very limited number of items, certain textiles, refrigerators and a few other miscellaneous items, against which the anti-dumping legislation has been applied since it was passed a few months ago. Surely, sir, it would be possible to list in very simple form the particular items, refrigerators, textiles and the rest, against which this legislation has been applied. List them by item, volume and prices, and then wind up with a statement of increases dollar-wise in duties which have been applied in an effort to protect the Canadian manufacturers, presumably, against those foreign imports.

We shall take note of the hon. gentleman's question and try to give him some information with reference to the query he has made. Perhaps it might satisfy him if we gave him typical examples rather than all the invoices and all the types of goods. I think what he wants is something to indicate what has been the general increase as a result of the policy which was adopted a few months ago.
That is right, sir. Could the minister not give us the information say on one particular type of refrigerator, any one, his choice, from the list he has there showing the duty?
I am afraid I have not that information with me.

Is there not another item against which the legislation has been applied on which the minister could give us information as to invoice price, appraised price for duty purposes and the increase in duty that has resulted?

Before the minister answers may I add a word? I myself was going to ask for something of that kind, because it seems to me that the figures we have now do not really carry conviction with them. It is reassuring to a point to take the December figures and the present figures and to infer from them that a lesson has been learned. It seems to me that if the minister could suggest one or two items in which we could have a comparison running back it would help. I should like to see a comparison not merely with the first four months of 1954 and December last, but with the first four months of 1954 perhaps with similar months of 1953. In any event, perhaps the minister and his officials can suggest some way in which this comparison could be made effective without all that work which I am sure none of us wishes to cause.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to ask a few questions about mixed fruit. I am still one of those simple souls who thinks that mixed fruit is mixed fruit and not peaches. That seems to have been the source of considerable argument, and I do not suppose the argument is over yet. I raise the matter because there are still one or two questions that I want to ask directly on the issue as to whether mixed fruit is peaches or not; also I want to question the way in which the Department of National Revenue is dealing with matters that come before the tariff board where the Department of National Revenue is involved. I recognize that the tariff board comes under the Minister of Finance, but my interest is not in the administration of the tariff board, but rather in the nature of the recommendations made to the tariff board by the Department of National Revenue.
Perhaps I might take just a moment to put on the record what has been the issue in respect of this question as to whether

mixed fruit is peaches or not. As I understand it, there are in the Customs Tariff several items which fix the rate of duty on peaches and on one or two other items of fruit. In all cases these are tins of fruit. Then there is the n.o.p. item, "not otherwise provided". It appears-
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, does the hon. gentleman think this matter ought to be discussed now when it is still before the court?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I would be interested to know if it is before the court.
Yes, it is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In what way?

It is still before the Exchequer Court, in that we have the right to make our appeal. Our appeal, if any, has not been heard at all. As far as the department goes, the importers made an appeal, and there was a judgment of the president of the Exchequer Court; but the department has the right to appeal, and that has not yet been heard.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: At the moment I am seeking information; I am not arguing.
That is the position.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us get this straight. As I understand it, there was an appeal from the tariff board to the Exchequer Court of Canada. The Exchequer Court issued its decision, in effect confirpning the decision of the tariff board. I do not know that there has yet been an appeal from the Exchequer Court ruling to the Supreme Court.

No, there has not been; there has been an appeal from the decision of the tariff board to the Exchequer Court by the department. Do not forget there are two parties to an action that comes before the tariff board. Here were the Department of National Revenue and the importer, and the tariff board gave a decision. The importers made an appeal to the Exchequer Court. That appeal has been dealt with. The Department of National Revenue has the right to make an appeal to the Exchequer Court.

speechtext: Order.

speechtext: May I add a word?

On the point of order; there are several lawyers around, including yourself, Mr. Chairman, and I would like to know what the situation is when a court has made a decision and no further appeal has been made. Is such a matter sub judice?

I am very happy to accept
both of your rulings. Have you been able, sir, to ascertain yet which item it is that has been fixed for the general discussion? I am prepared to defer this discussion to that other item if I can be told which one it is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Wishes to say a few things and ask a few questions.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is only fair to mention that the Leader of the Opposition made it quite clear, in the point he raised, that he was asking questions which he thought related to the matter under discussion, namely the application of the December amendment in relation to dumping. He made his statement and said he was asking these questions as they applied to the particular subject which was agreed to be the subject for discussion this morning. speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might proceed with his general remarks. If I interrupt him at about the same point in his remarks that I did in the case of the Leader of the Opposition, we may find that he too intends to observe the understanding.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not too sure as to the meaning of that remark, but I am in a very co-operative mood this morning, and the leader of the house can confirm that, because these arrangements have been changed so often this morning that I have forgotten how many times they have been made and upset.
However, Mr. Chairman, I shall not take very many minutes to deal with this matter. I do not intend to debate the issue of whether mixed fruit is peaches. The department ruled one way and that ruling was that mixed fruit should be classified as peaches and the effect of that was to increase the duty. The case was taken to the tariff board and the tariff board ruled against the department. Their ruling was to the effect


%
that mixed fruit was mixed fruit and should be charged the duty provided under n.o.p.- not otherwise provided.
The case went from the tariff board to the Exchequer Court and the Exchequer Court refused leave to appeal against the tariff board decision which had the effect of confirming the tariff board decision that mixed fruit is mixed fruit and not peaches. Where it goes from there we do not yet know.
However, there is a question of administration or policy involved in this on which I wish to say a few words. When the case was heard before the tariff board it turned out that the representations on behalf of the Department of National Revenue were made not by officers of the Department of National Revenue but by a person from the Department of Justice. It also turns out, and I have had the privilege of reading the transcript of the evidence, that in the discussion that took place-if I may put it this way-the ground was shifted two or three times.
The other side to the case appeared before the tariff board prepared to argue against the contention that mixed fruit was peaches. During the discussion the representative of the Department of Justice suggested to the tariff board that perhaps the ruling made by the Department of National Revenue was wrong, that perhaps mixed fruit should be regarded as preserves, and if that was not a satisfactory proposition then perhaps mixed fruit should be put into another basket item in the customs tariff schedule.
The result of that, Mr. Chairman, was that the people on the other side did not know where they stood. The ground was being shifted and arguments were being advanced that were not in the original proposition. It seems to me that that way of dealing with the matter is quite unfair. I recognize the fact that the position I would take was finally taken by the tariff board, when it ruled that mixed fruit should still be n.o.p., and at the moment that is the decision unless an appeal is made to the Supreme Court. But if the decision stands then somewhere along the line it looks as though there will have to be rebates of rather substantial sums.
On one occasion on the orders of the day I asked the Minister of National Revenue whether it was the intention of the Department of National Revenue to continue this practice of having a representative of the Department of Justice represent the Department of National Revenue in these hearings before the tariff board. Indeed, it is on that point that I would like him to comment. On that occasion he gave the short answer "Yes". But it seems to me that this is an unfair way

of dealing with this matter. When the case comes before the tariff board it makes it very difficult for the opposite side when someone comes in from the Department of Justice and shifts the ground considerably, as was done in this case, so that the other party does not know what arguments they will have to answer.
It seems to me, if one can think of this in the sense of court procedure, that that is hardly a fair way to deal with it. I am sure the Minister of National Revenue is familiar with all the facts of the case and I would appreciate it if he would comment on that particular matter, namely the way in which the Department of National Revenue makes its representations to the tariff board when a ruling of the department has been appealed to that board.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the hon. gentleman's question I could give him a little of the background here in connection with the lawyers who appeared before the tariff board. They began appearing early in the life of the present tariff board. As a matter of fact, a lawyer was involved in one of the cases heard on April 25, 1949, and that was appealed, although I need not go into the details. On May 18 there was an appeal before the board, and in 1949 three lawyers represented the appellant in appeal case No. 177. There are numerous other instances I could give which would serve to indicate that lawyers have appeared in all the cases since the very beginning. The first time that the Department of National Revenue used a lawyer there was on June 7, 1950, on appeal No. 214. If the hon. member wishes to know if it is our intention to continue to use lawyers the answer is yes, and the Department of Justice being the legal advisers to every government department we propose to use their services when required.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Supply-National Revenue

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-Loans, investments and advances-
534. Loans to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation repayable with interest at a rate to be fixed by the governor in council on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine and to be applied in payment of expenditures to cover capital costs of television installations and to support the development of the service. Such loans, with interest, shall be a charge on the revenues of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation next after the charge imposed under the provisions of section 17 of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, $3,000,000.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that that procedure is quite agreeable to me. This particular item has to do with a loan to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for television installation. In this statement I have laid stress on the television side of broadcasting rather than sound broadcasting. However, it does open up the matter for discussion.
This item covers a proposed loan to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for capital expenditures on television installations. The committee will recall that last year parliament approved a loan of $4,750,000 to the corporation towards the cost of building television facilities in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Ottawa and Halifax, together with a transmitter in Montreal. The loan last year, as was explained at the time, represented only part of the cost of the program, with the remainder to be met by a further loan in this fiscal year. The amount proposed this year is $3 million and it will cover the remainder of the cost of the projects that were approved last year.
As hon. members are aware, we are in the midst of a wide development of television broadcasting in Canada. The C.B.C. began operating its production centres and stations at Montreal and Toronto in September, 1952.
I would point out that that is less than two years since our first station was opened. Just over a year ago these stations were linked together by direct network connection. The Ottawa station went on the air at about the same time. The C.B.C. station in Vancouver opened last December. The second transmitter in Montreal began functioning in January of this year. The Winnipeg station will go on the air in a few days and the Halifax station is expected to start before the end of the present year. At the same time the number and variety of television programs has been greatly increased. The growing interest in the country is shown by the fact


that about three-quarters of a million families are reported to have bought television sets in Canada, and it is expected that sales this year will considerably exceed those of last fiscal year when some 400,000 sets were sold.
There are also at the moment four private stations operating, with more expected to be on the air shortly. All are functioning as members of the national system and are being supplied by the C.B.C. with national program service which is amounting to from 20 to 28 hours a week.
During this year there will be further wide expansion in the television system. The C.B.C. is developing program production facilities at the regional points of Vancouver, Winnipeg, and Halifax, and will have some facilities for live output in Ottawa. In addition 16 more private stations are already authorized and will be coming on the air at different times-it is expected most of them before the end of the year. The C.B.C. will be supplying all the private stations in addition to its own with national program service.
The C.B.C. is now supplying service to the private stations at London and Kitchener by direct network connection. It is planned that such direct connections would be established with all stations in southern Ontario and Quebec just as soon as they go on the air. Stations in other parts of the country for the time being will be supplied by means of kinescope recordings. As the number of stations increase this will entail greatly expanded facilities for the making and handling of recordings. The C.B.C. is looking forward to direct network connections across the country from coast to coast, and has already asked for tenders from communication companies for extensions of network service both east and west from central Canada. Such a national direct network system will of course involve commitments for heavy annual payments by the corporation.
Because of the high sales of sets, revenues to the C.B.C. from the 15 per cent excise tax on the wholesale price of receiving sets has been actually higher than was anticipated at the beginning of the last fiscal year. The proceeds of the tax applying to television amounted to approximately $11,700,000 for 1953-54. I am sorry that since its fiscal year has just recently closed, the annual statement of the corporation is not yet available. The corporation estimates that on the television side they will show an operating surplus of some $5 million. This television operating surplus from last year has been all earmarked by the corporation for further capital expenditures, and will to this amount reduce the need for further capital loans in

the future. The funds will be used to provide additional technical and production facilities, which are being made necessary for the development of the system. The present program facilities are being taxed beyond capacity to provide the number of Canadian productions at present being broadcast. With increasing pressure for the carrying of more non-Canadian programs, it has become more and more necessary to add to the facilities for producing Canadian programs. I think all the hon. members will agree that at least a reasonable proportion of our television broadcasting should be provided by Canadians for Canadians.
In this way the surplus which the corporation will show in television for the past fiscal year will be plowed back into facilities for maintaining and improving the national television service right across the country.
It is not very expensive to import television programs in Canada and put them on our television stations; it is extremely expensive to produce television programs ourselves in Canada. And it is also expensive to link the different parts of the country together by television. I think we all realize that television is bound to have a very great effect on our family and national life and particularly on the growing minds of young Canadians. At the same time we have to face the fact that the development of a Canadian system, broadcasting at least a reasonable proportion of Canadian programs, spreading across the country from coast to coast, is going to cost a great deal of money to operate. At the present time in Canada we are developing one of the most extensive television systems in the world. It represents one of the great developments in the history of our country and it is being built under a scheme of sensible co-operation between public and private interest. I believe that in television we in Canada must think in big national terms, not just weighing individual local considerations. And if we continue to think and plan for the national interest, in the interests of Canadians in all parts of the country, we are going to have a television system of which we as a nation can be justly proud.

Mr. Chairman, the committee is hampered this year in its approach to the consideration of the various items affecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by the fact that there has been no committee of the house this year reviewing the operations of the corporation, and also by reason of the fact that the corporation's annual report is not in our hands.
It has been the practice throughout the two last previous parliaments that a special
4, 1954
' Supply-National Revenue committee of the house should be set up in alternate sessions to review the operations of the corporation. The committee did sit in the session of 1953, and I have no doubt one will sit during the next session of parliament. Certainly we in this part of the house will be asking that such a committee be appointed at the next session.
Then, as to the annual report, I would call to the attention of the hon. members the fact that the fiscal year of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation follows the fiscal year of the government, ending on March 31. It is unfortunate that in a year when there has been no special committee reviewing the operations of the corporation, and its policies, we have not before us at this time any report of the operations of the corporation, since the one which closed with the date March 31, 1953. Here we are more than 14 months later and, apart from the somewhat brief review the minister has given to the committee, we know virtually nothing as to the financial operations of the corporation during the past 14 months. As the situation may arise in the future, I think some consideration should be given either to expediting the annual report for occasions such as this, or probably considering the possibility of making the fiscal year of the corporation coincide with the calendar year, rather than with the fiscal year of the government. I am making no further comments as to the feasibility of this suggestion. It is the sort of thing that can be discussed with the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation when a special committee next sits. But we are left in the position today where we are without the benefit of the work done by a committee, and without access to any report since that of March 31, 1953. Therefore our information in approaching the estimates affecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is quite inadequate.
Sir, we have a half dozen items before us. As the minister mentioned in his remarks, there are two items on page 8 which are of a statutory nature. The first is $6,250,000 to provide for the requirements of the sound broadcasting service. The second is an item of $15 million to provide for payment to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation from the consolidated revenue fund of amounts equal to the taxes collected under the Excise Tax Act in respect of radio and television sets and equipment. Then we have item 534, immediately under debate, to provide the sum of $3 million by way of loans to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to cover capital costs of television installations and to support the development of the service. There are

Supply-National Revenue of course the other items which relate specifically to the international shortwave service, which I shall not deal with in these somewhat general remarks at this stage.
I should like to draw to the attention of the committee at the outset, sir, the fact that the bulk of the money going from the consolidated revenue fund of this country into the coffers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is going there not by direct vote of this house now but under authority of a statute passed previously. We in this part of the house took issue with the method that was proposed by the government last year, and indeed on previous occasions, in this respect. Provisions of a continuing nature were made at the insistence of the government both in the years 1951 and 1953. In the year 1951, to implement one of the proposals of the Massey royal commission, the government asked the house to make a continuing five-year grant to the corporation of $6,250,000 a year. In 1953, when the licence fee of $2.50 on radio receiving sets was abolished, a nuisance tax which we in this part of the house had attacked vigorously for many years, provision was made for substituting revenue on a much more generous scale by way of allocating to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the annual proceeds of the excise tax collected on the sale of radio and television receiving sets in Canada. At that time we were told the estimated revenue from that source for a full year would be approximately $12 million. In the case of the 1951 vote, it was set up on a five-year basis. In the case of the 1953 vote, it is set up on an indefinite basis that can go on in perpetuity unless legislation to the contrary is passed in this house.
We in the official opposition took issue with that type of indefinite provision, and we still do. We are prepared to deal on its merits with any provision, any grant or any loan that we are asked to vote in favour of the corporation to assist its work either in the field of sound or television broadcasting; but we do not believe that this matter of providing indefinite grants, continuing year after year without any control or direct vote on the part of parliament, can by any stretch of the imagination be harmonized with a proper appreciation of the importance of parliamentary control over the expenditure of public moneys.
We have been given some indication from the minister this afternoon that the estimate given to the house last year as to the revenue which was expected from the tax on radio and television receiving sets has been exceeded. We have not been given the figures as to the breakdown between the
[Mr. Fleming.1

television and the radio sets. I should think it would not be very difficult to obtain those figures on a breakdown basis.
It will be recalled, sir, that the Massey royal commission recommended that the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in their financial aspects, should be carefully separated as between sound broadcasting on the one hand and television broadcasting on the other. Last year, when the government's proposal came before the house, it was suggested to us that of the $12 million of expected revenue, the amounts yielded would be approximately equal as between radio broadcasting and television broadcasting. We in the official opposition asked for a clear and definite allocation to be established by legislation so that revenue from tax on the sale of radio receiving sets would be allocated to sound broadcasting and revenue derived from taxes on the sale of television sets would be allocated to the purposes of television. But in the result, the government would not accept this proposal and insisted that the revenue derived from the tax on both sound receiving sets and television sets should be mingled.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the first thing we want to know is what is the breakdown of revenue as between the tax on radio receiving sets on the one hand and on the television sets on the other. We will want to know in a way that is just not possible without a detailed operating statement of the corporation for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954 before us, what have been the revenues received and what have been the expenditures upon sound broadcasting and television broadcasting, both fully separated.
We should have a proper and detailed statement as to the use made by the corporation of the substantial sums of money which were placed at its disposal during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954. Actually, the revenues at their disposal in both fields of sound and television broadcasting for that fiscal year aggregated some $26,750,000. I gave the detail of that breakdown on May 14, 1953, at page 5418 of Hansard, in reviewing the work of the special committee on radio broadcasting for that year, and the information it had gathered as to the financial operations and plans of the corporation.
I make it quite clear now that I am asking for a detailed breakdown in this committee now of that substantial total of $26,750,000, by far the largest sum ever placed at the disposal of the corporation in any fiscal year, indeed, several times larger than the figures available to it in recent years.

We come again, sir, to the question of loans. This house, over a period of several years, has already placed at the disposal of the corporation a total of $8 million by way of loans for the development of television. One might have thought that with the very largely increased sums available to the corporation from the proceeds of the excise tax on radio receiving sets and television sets there would be no occasion for the corporation to come back to parliament for further loans. After all, with $26,750,000 available for all purposes last year, and with the information now that the estimate of $12 million given to the house at that time as to the expected revenue from the proceeds of the excise tax on receiving sets and television sets is less than the amount actually realized, one would think that there would not be occasion to come back to parliament asking for more loans; yet we are being asked now to provide a loan of an additional $3 million to cover the capital cost of television installations and to support the development of the service.
The house, Mr. Chairman, has been given no adequate explanation of this item, and I call upon the minister for infinitely more information than he has yet imparted to the house to justify this substantial loan, in addition to all the other revenues that are available to the corporation from the various sources which have been allotted to it by parliament.
Let me remind the house, sir, as to what some of those revenues are which are now regularly available to the corporation. We have, first of all, the excise tax and it is to be observed that this year the statutory item with respect to the proceeds of the excise tax stands at $15 million. That, in itself, is an increase of $3 million over the estimate of $12 million upon which the house proceeded at the 1953 session. In addition there is the continuing grant of $6,250,000 under the program approved by parliament in 1951. In addition to these two sources, Mr. Chairman, there are still available to the corporation its revenues from commercial broadcasting. Indeed, we have not been given the figures of revenue from commercial broadcasting for this past fiscal year, but on reference to the annual report of the corporation for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953, we may see that the revenue from commercial broadcasting in that year exceeded $2,500,000 from sound broadcasting, and even in the very limited operation in the television field I find that for the fiscal year there had been received a total of $518,000 by way of commercial revenue in respect of television broadcasting.

Now, with the very largely increased program of television operations carried on by the corporation in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, it must be apparent that the revenues to the corporation from commercial broadcasting must be very much larger than that and would aggregate something in excess of $3 million. There are some other items of revenue as well.
I draw attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that these are very substantial sources of revenue to the corporation, and now, more than ever before in our history, when dealing with the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its operations, we are dealing with an organization whose claims upon the public treasury are becoming ever greater and now reach into very substantial amounts which call on the part of parliament for the strictest review and the exercise of the fullest parliamentary control.
Mention has been made, sir, of the way in which the public has been purchasing receiving sets. Indeed, sir, the rate at which the public has been purchasing television sets has been extraordinary. In the year 1954, according to the dominion bureau of statistics' daily bulletin for March 26, we learn that manufacturers' sales of television receivers soared to as high as 366,498 units in the full year 1953 compared with 137,236 in 1952. In other words, sir, the total television receiving sets sold in Canada in 1953 were almost three times the number sold in Canada in 1952. Radio sales rose more moderately to 620,800 in 1953 from 568,844 in the year 1952. The value of the TV sets sold in 1953 was $148,753,000 compared with $60,659,000 in 1952, and radio sales were valued at $52,119,000 compared with $50,125,000 in the year 1952.
The sale of TV sets by areas in Canada in 1953 is also striking. In the Atlantic provinces it was only 869; in Quebec 119,519; in Ontario 225,726; in the prairie provinces 1,270; and in British Columbia 19,114. The extraordinary rate of public purchases of television sets is continuing in 1954, according to the figures issued by the RadioTelevision Manufacturers Association of Canada which reported that the sale of television sets for the first four months of 1954 amounted to 137,267 compared with 94,136 in a like period in 1953. In respect of the sale of sound receiving sets, sales for the first four months of 1954 totalled 142,517 units compared with 198,021 units in the like period of 1953.
It will be observed from these figures, Mr. Chairman, that the tendency now is for the sales of the radio receiving sets to decline.

Now, sir, I turn from the subject of finance, knowing that we have been given only the scratchiest and sketchiest kind of information, quite inadequate for the needs of the house in facing its responsibilities in regard to the substantial amounts that are now under consideration, to the question of policy, which is a matter of high importance.
There have been extensive debates in this house on the subject in relation to both sound broadcasting and television for years past.
I am not going to suggest that there is any occasion now to cover all the ground that has been covered in other years. But I wish to make several facts plain, so far as the policy to which we subscribe is concerned, as well as to make quite clear what I deem to be the inevitable effects of the policy now being pursued by the government in relation to the licensing of stations, and in particular of television stations.
In the first place, sir, we have in the government's policy a point-blank contradiction as between its policy on sound broadcasting on the one hand and television broadcasting on the other.
Bet me take as my illustration the testimony of Mr. Browne, an official of the Department of Transport, before the special committee on broadcasting of the 1953 session. I quoted this in my remarks in the debate on May 14, 1953, as can be found at page 5419 of Hansard. This is the question I put to him:
You say there Is no policy against licensing-
This is for sound broadcasting, Mr. Chairman.
-two or more stations in the same area?
The answer was:
There is no government policy which restricts the number of stations of which I am aware.
That was the testimony of an official in the Department of Transport through whom the function of the licensing of stations is exercised. It is quite clear that there is no government policy against the licensing of more than one station in areas where there are existing stations in the field of sound broadcasting. Mr. Chairman, the result is that, apart from what our views may be with


regard to the regulation of sound broadcasting in general, we at least do not have to attack a policy of local monopoly in favour of existing stations. At any rate, the government's policy, whatever may have been its shortcomings, in the field of sound broadcasting has not been open to that criticism.
We still have our views, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the whole method of control and regulation of radio broadcasting in Canada. We consider it to be unsound in its nature that the system should call for the operation of a national system on the part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and that at the same time the corporation, clothed with that responsibility, should be charged also with the responsibility of and be given the wide powers of regulation over all other broadcasting in Canada. There are many private stations in Canada. Our view was and continues to be that the proper method of regulating broadcasting in Canada would be through a separate board which would be a public board, fully responsible to parliament, discharging a public responsibility, but clothed with the responsibility and power needed in relation to the regulation of all forms of broadcasting in Canada, whether they are publicly or privately owned stations. We do not think that the best results are obtained by having a corporation which is charged with the duty of operating in the national field also being given these broad regulatory powers. The two functions are separate and distinct and, in our submission, they should be discharged by separate bodies in the same way as the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada exercises the powers vested in it under the Railway Act over both the privately-owned Canadian Pacific Railway and the publicly-owned Canadian National Railways. It is a system of that kind that we think would be best suited to the needs of Canada in this important field of communications.
I come now to the field of government policy in relation to television broadcasting. Here I think one can best illustrate government policy by placing side by side with the description of policy given by Mr. Browne, in the passage that I have just quoted from his evidence which was given something over a year ago, a question following in the same gentleman's testimony. I asked him this question:
Q. In other words, it is not the policy to foster a local monopoly in sound broadcasting?-A. There is no government policy, as I have said, akin to that which at the present time applies in the case of
television.
Sir, the policy of the government in relation to television is to foster a series of local monopolies in Canada. Along with that

policy has gone the policy of fostering a monopoly for the publicly-owned stations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the large cities-the metropolitan areas- where there has been the greatest demand, actually, for the establishment of more television outlets. The inevitable results of this policy which the government has stubbornly followed have been, first of all, to delay for years the introduction of television in Canada and, now that television has been introduced into Canada, as it was introduced in a rather modified form a year and a half or two years ago and, so far as the publicly-owned system is concerned, is now being extended by rather slow degrees to deny at the same time to other areas that service in the field of television which they desire and which at the same time many organizations are prepared to risk their capital to provide. The reason that many areas in this country are still denied any television and further the reason that areas in this country which have limited television today are denied more opportunities of having alternative television services is that the government has stubbornly followed this policy first of delaying the development of television and now of fostering local monopoly.
We of the Progressive Conservative party do not believe in any policy of local monopoly. We believe that the best results will be achieved not only for those who wish to receive additional programs but in the whole aspect of the relationship between parliament and public authority on the one hand and operations in this field on the other, if competition is not discouraged, as the government is deliberately discouraging it.
We are not alone in holding that view. Others have put that view forward. Indeed, organizations within the Liberal party itself have publicly declared that view before now. I take you back, Mr. Chairman, to November 11, 1951, when the Young Liberal Federation of Canada in its meeting at Vancouver, according to a Canadian Press dispatch of that date from Vancouver, asked the government to establish an independent administration to control radio and television, including the C.B.C. I come forward to October 27, 1952, when a Canadian Press dispatch of that date reports that the advisory council of the Liberal federation, which is described as the high command of the federal party in power, passed this resolution:
"Recognizing that the use of radio has become universal in Canada . . .
And so on. They recommended abolition of the radio licence fee. That recommendation was carried out. That fact leads me to ask

I have drawn attention to what is an eloquent comment on the feeling within the Liberal party about the Liberal government's policy of monopoly. Now, sir, I turn to remarks which I think are entitled to very great respect. They come from a gentleman for whom I have learned to have a high regard in the frequent contacts I have
TMr. Fleming.]
had with him as a member of the house and as a member of the special committee on radio broadcasting from year to year since I came into the house in 1945. It is Mr. Davidson Dunton, the chairman of the board of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, whom I regard as a very conscientious official of that corporation. In a recent address which Mr. Dunton made in Saskatoon on May 14, 1954, he faced up in a very frank way, it seemed to me, to the problem of trying to reconcile freedom of expression and freedom of communication on the one hand with regulation in the field of sound and television broadcasting on the other. I shall quote a couple of passages from his speech, and I think hon. members will listen to them with interest. After referring to the early origin of the struggle for freedom of speech he says:
But conditions have changed since the early days of the original fights for freedom of expression. Now a relatively small number of great printing presses turn out a large part of the actual reading material of most people. A few transmitting stations put out all the broadcasting heard effectively by the population of a whole region. A handful of men control the making of most moving pictures seen by millions. In effect a small number of men -publishers, broadcasters, film organization heads- can control a large part of the ideas and impressions and opinions that reach the minds of most people.
I think that if we are realistic we have to admit that an inherent danger to a genuinely free and fair interchange of ideas has developed from the concentration of so much power over means of mass communication in the hands of so few. I am very conscious of this myself because I and others of the C.B.C. belong to the few, together with controllers of publishing, film and other broadcasting organizations.
Further down he says:
There is true freedom in mass communication only if ideas which happen to appeal to lesser numbers of people have a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Then people as a whole have a chance to weigh and choose, and perhaps change their minds, for themselves. The essence of freedom lies in freedom to choose from a variety of alternatives; if there are no alternatives-in kinds of ideas and material presented-there can be no freedom of choice.
I think that final sentence from Mr. Dunton's speech is one that deserves to be echoed.
The essence of freedom lies in freedom to choose from a variety of alternatives; if there are no alternatives-in kinds of ideas and material presented-there can be no freedom of choice.
Please do not misunderstand what I am saying on this point, Mr. Chairman. I am not saying that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation does not attempt to provide a variety of ideas or a variety of programs, but I am saying that no one organization can fulfil the specifications of freedom laid down in this penetrating observation of Mr. Dunton

if the ideas are coming from one organization or in local areas from one station or one source. That is why this policy of fostering monopoly is fraught with the utmost dangers. It is a policy that has run too long. It is a policy that, in my submission, must be abandoned. It is true that you cannot force people to listen over the air. Listeners retain the freedom to turn the dials and shut off the machine. But the fact of the matter is that as long as it is government policy to attempt to confine people to one source in this rapidly developing means of communication, television, the effects and influence of which on the minds and lives of people are simply incalculable, we are courting a danger to the very fundamentals of our whole conception of freedom.
I do urge upon the house that the house address itself to the imminent, pressing perils for Canadians of a policy of monopoly which this government has deliberately followed, has deliberately fostered and to which it still unrepentantly adheres. This policy must be put aside. The government must cease to impose monopoly upon the people. Encouragement should be given, with all the safeguards that are available under law, to permitting people to have alternative sources of communication in this important and rapidly expanding field. The time has come, Mr. Chairman, for a drastic change in our policy in relation to regulation in this field.

Mr. Chairman, this estimate always provides an occasion to discuss matters concerning the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I may say that usually during the preceding year I have had the opportunity to view and hear a good many of the programs or have been directed to them and have heard them pretty thoroughly discussed by someone who listened constantly. This year I am not quite in that position, but in spite of the criticisms that have just been levelled against the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I want to remind the committee-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman: I thought my criticisms were directed against government policy, and I expressly dissociated the C.B.C. from the policy that was imposed upon them.

It is very difficult to distinguish between criticism of government policy in this field and criticism of the corporation itself. After all I want to say to my hon. friend that the foundation of this system was laid not by the C.C.F. nor by the Liberals, but by the government of the late R. B. Bennett and the Conservative party. When Mr. Bennett introduced a 83276-349

As I said, I am not so familiar personally with the programs this year as I have been in other years, but when I look at the record of what our broadcasting corporation has done throughout the years, particularly during the past year, I find this. Considering the record of television first, I may say that a year ago this week, June 2, 1953, I had the privilege of witnessing that remarkable television account of the coronation. I thought it was handled by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and by the B.B.C. of course, with dignity. It was something of which the B.B.C., the C.B.C., and of course the R.A.F. and the R.C.A.F., who made possible the quick transmissions of the films to Canada, can be proud. As a matter of fact, I noted that program was awarded the Sylvania television award for 1953, which is a presentation by the Sylvania Electric Products Corporation. . . . for more than speed. It includes our recognition of the dignity and good taste, in keeping with the solemnity of the subject displayed by ABC, and we tender our thanks to the BBC for its initiation of service and to the CBC for its part in retransmission.
As one of those who witnessed that program, and perhaps because of my own church affiliation, I appreciated the fact that the coronation itself was introduced into what is perhaps the most solemn and beautiful service of the Anglican communion, and I felt very pleased indeed with what was done in that regard.
