I feel we have to bear this in mind, that television and radio are monopolies. To the organizations operating these stations, we allocate airways. No one else can use those airways, so once we allocate them they are monopolies. In my opinion, since it is a natural monopoly, it should be under public control. My hon. friend criticizes this monopoly, but I should like to hear him criticize some other monopolies in this country. I should like to hear him criticize the Bell Telephone Company in this part of the world. I should like to hear him criticize the Aluminum Company of Canada. I should like to hear him criticize the International Nickel Company, and a number of monopolies that exist in this country, and which no attempt has been made to curb. If we are going to have criticism of what is a natural monopoly, which I think we must keep under public control, then by the same token surely we should see to it that we curb private monopolies that are not natural monopolies even if they are built up on the natural resources of the country.
I mentioned the coronation program because I believe it made a very deep impression on all the people who witnessed the dignity of the service, and the manner in which the film was presented in contrast with the manner in which it was presented in the United States. One of the great broadcasting organizations there introduced a gorilla or chimpanzee in the middle of the program to advertise a private product. This indicates the extent to which private organizations will sometimes go in order to display advertising.
Another thing that I have in mind is that I noticed the minister said that private television stations-I am not saying that there


should not be private television stations-are being supplied with productions by the C.B.C., and that some of these will have to be supplied with kinescope. I am asking the minister this question. What revenue does the C.B.C. derive when it supplies these private stations with programs that must cost the C.B.C. a great deal of money to produce. To what extent do they pay for the films that are made available by the C.B.C.? It seems to me that if we are thinking of television, we should know something about that. When we have a direct network program across Canada supplying programs to both private and public stations, as the minister intimated that is going to be very costly. I feel we should go into the division of costs very thoroughly indeed.
May I add that I was talking a few days ago to a gentleman for whom I have quite a lot of respect, who operates a station of which I have some knowledge and which is a good private station. He was asked if he was going into television. He said he did not know, because after all it would cost from $250,000 to a half million to set up a television station in the area where he lived. I venture to say that only big money can put stations of that description into operation. And if we are going to rely entirely on big accumulations of money to build our television stations we shall be in the same position as we are in some areas of this country where we have only one outlet in the form of newspapers-areas where there are single newspapers owning broadcasting facilities and moulding public opinion, just as well as attempting to control it in the areas in which they operate.
It seems to me that if we are going to have freedom of the press, freedom of opinion and the like, we must consider this matter very carefully. And then I think that, so far as I have been able to see, both in its television and in its sound broadcasting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is trying to give to us various types of opinion, however they may differ. And these opinions are expressed over radio and television. As all of us know, from time to time there have been complaints about the freedom of speech that has been exercised on the C.B.C. national broadcasting system.
I listened to the extract from the speech delivered in Saskatoon by Mr. Davidson Dun-ton, and quoted by the hon. member for Eglinton, and my interpretation of that speech was somewhat different from that placed upon it by my hon. friend. I think what the chairman of the broadcasting corporation was pleading for was more tolerance and more free speech on the radio. I venture to ask this question: Would that be obtained

or assured if there were private control of television and radio in this country? I venture to say it would not. Moreover, when the Massey commission reported to the house -upon which the present policy of the house, not the government, is based-it made these very points to which I now refer.
Let me now say something about Canadian talent. This year we have not had a radio committee. I suppose that probably we shall have one next year. I think it is a good thing to have the broadcasting corporation appear before a parliamentary committee. However, because we have not had a committee, we do not know to what extent Canadian talent is being used by private stations. We know that when the committee met in former years we were told that very little encouragement was given to private talent by some-not all-of the private stations in Canada. It was shown that, as a matter of fact, private talent was largely developed through the C.B.C.
There are one or two exceptions to this. I would like to pay my respects again to a private company, Canadian Industries Limited, for its very remarkable program in developing private talent, "Singing Stars of Tomorrow". I have often wished that program had been undertaken by the C.B.C.; but I suppose, owing to the fact that a substantial sum of money is given as awards, it might have been the subject of criticism in the house.
They get a deduction in their income tax.

My hon. friend says that they get a deduction in their income tax, which the C.B.C. would not get. However, be that as it may, let me pay my respects again to that most excellent and interesting program. After all, such programs are important; because if we are going to build up the kind of Canada in which many of us believe, a Canada which will be prosperous materially, we must have a Canada that will match its material prosperity by its cultural development. If we are to be an independent nation, free from control by the ideas of the great nation to the south, then it seems to me most important that we have an organization that will control the kind of programs we get over television and over radio, to see that they are Canadian in background and in outlook.
Because, as we all know, radio and television are potent means of propaganda and education. I was not here when the radio broadcasting commission was set up, but I was here when the present corporation was set up. I believe those who established the commission had the same views as those who set up the corporation. And certainly those who voted for the corporation in 1936 held the view that what we were trying to do was to promote a Canadian system of broadcasting which would be used to build up the national life and culture of this country.
Now, I want to say something about revenues. It is quite true, as the hon. member for Eglinton has said, that the amount collected under the excise from the sale of television and radio sets now going to the C.B.C. has assumed very considerable proportions-larger than was estimated last year. We have had tremendous developments in television in Canada, and we may have even greater developments in the next few years. So long as people are buying radio and television sets, the C.B.C. will have very considerable revenue. But there will come a saturation point, surely; and when that saturation point comes it seems to me parliament will be faced with a problem.

I suppose it is very difficult to give breakdowns today because we have not got the final report of the operations of the corporation for the last year. That is the advantage of a radio committee. Across the floor of this house we indulge in debate on various phases of government policy or of government operation. But when we get the corporation or the organization before a parliamentary committee, with the officials there who can speak for themselves, we can go into these matters much more thoroughly.
There are other programs that I have not mentioned this afternoon that are of great value. School broadcasts and the manner in which they are undertaken, for example, are a great aid to the schools of Canada. I hope that they will not only be continued but will be expanded. I want to say that I personally have confidence in the general work that the corporation is doing and for which we are paying. It is true that in various areas the corporation must of necessity have a monopoly in the district because, as I have indicated, television is such an expensive operation, and the cost of producing programs so great that if we are to have the type of program we must have, we cannot have half a dozen trying to produce programs and using available facilities to produce programs that are inferior to what might be done through joint public effort. It seems to me that is one of the great advantages of having the kind of television we have at the present time. The awards to which I referred, given in the United States for our Canadian radio and television programs, are eloquent tribute to what is being done. Of course great improvement is possible. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope that a committee will be set up next year, and instead of our talking across the floor, without all the information we should have at our fingertips, we can go into the operations of the corporation much more thoroughly than we can this year.

We are happy once again to be able to join in this debate in respect to the appropriations now being voted for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, both in the sound radio field and in the television field. Over the years we have voted a tremendous amount of money for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We are now called upon


once again to vote considerable sums for that organization. We have not vigorously opposed the voting of moneys to this corporation, but one thing we do want to make plain is that when we are voting such moneys for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is a government-owned corporation, it must expect to be open to criticism, perhaps serious criticism, and sometimes harsh criticism. I am quite sure, because of the fact that those in authority in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are human, as we all are, they may, because of human tendencies, resent some criticism; yet on the other hand I am quite sure they are men who would appreciate honest, fair and constructive criticism.
We are not the only ones in parliament of course who are critics of radio and television policy. We have found that the press of this country have also been critics of the present government policy with respect to radio and television. Not so very long ago an article appeared in Maclean's magazine. I do not know whether the minister would care to comment at all on the article, whether it is a correct appraisal of the situation, or whether it is out of line. I do not expect the minister to take account of everything that is written in the press of Canada with respect to government radio policy. If he took time to do that, perhaps he would not be doing very much else. The article did contain an appraisal and an analysis- although of course it was critical-of present radio and television. It applied particularly to television policy in Canada. The criticism appearing in Maclean's magazine, I believe in the early April issue, was written by Mr. Scott Young. It was based on the fundamental principle that government control of television and broadcasting is precisely the same as government control of the press and publications generally; that such control is a well recognized feature of dictatorship, whether communism, fascist, or nazi, and therefore has no place in a free country.
In his analysis Mr. Young pointed out what the government's aims really were in respect to television policy. He lists three or four of them. One is, it is supposed to serve all tastes. Another is to keep television Canadian in belief and ideas with the allied point of subduing United States influence. Quite a lot of discussion has taken place about United States influence. Perhaps it is partly justified, I do not know; but I am not so frightened as some appear to be of the influence that might come to us from our good neighbours to the south, although there are some practices there relating to television and radio that I would not want to see adopted here. I hope parliamentary

committee investigations will not be televised. It lowers the dignity of our parliamentary institutions, and it does no particular good to portray in this dramatic fashion the entire truth of those investigations. I think very largely that in the United States in televising the various congressional committees, such as the Kefauver crime committee of a few years ago, and the recent committee on subversive influences, the intentions of the authorities may have been good, but it has eventually worked out to be rather a dramatic farce. I hope personally the time will never come when such a thing is repeated in this parliament.
However, on the broad principles I am not so worried as some people seem to be with respect to American influence in this country as far as radio and television are concerned. As a matter of fact, we are having it now; we have always had it; and some of the best and most popular programs over our networks, and this will probably be the case over our television networks for years to come, are American productions.
Another thing Mr. Young lists here as government intention as regards TV is to maintain good taste, and in addition to avoid commercial influence while making television pay its way. Mr. Young points out in his article that these objectives have not been reached by any stretch of the imagination.
For example, he analyses a weekend review of television which might be seen on any television station. I will quote from the article I have here in my hand which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, and which is more or less a summary of Mr. Young's article. He states:
For instance, if the week were average and they were watching CBLT-Toronto they would see about 65 hours of television. They would see 17 elderly movies, mostly American and some quite good, and in the time not taken up by movies they would see 24 commercial programs produced in the United States and sponsored here by American companies whose products also sell in Canada.
They would see six Canadian commercially sponsored programs, a fraction of the number C.B.C. had hoped to sell. On a time basis, only about 45 per cent of what they saw would originate in Canada, . . .
That shows how far we have fallen short of making our TV really Canadian. On a time basis only 45 per cent of what they saw would originate in Canada.
... 50 per cent or more in the United States, the rest in Britain-a very broad interpretation of the C.B.C.'s feeling that a majority of its programs should be of Canadian content.
Mr. Young also analyses the financial picture as to what might have been expected
Supply-National Revenue according to the announcements made previously by the appropriate authorities, including the minister. He states:
Of the $22 million spent by C.B.C.-TV in its first 19 months of operation, the $11 million for capital outlay must be considered a long term investment. But a return of $1,750,000 in advertising revenue for the remaining $11 million of operating costs is a figure that has only one explanation. No one ever should have expected, let alone promised, that TV under the C.B.C. system could ever pay its own way.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the previous speeches made here this afternoon on this item and I quite realize that the speech of the spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party and that of the leader of the C.C.F. ran true to form. I do not blame the leader of the C.C.F. for taking the attitude in his speech that he has always taken over the years, because he thinks of all things in terms of a socialist concept. Nor can I blame him for supporting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in practically everything it does. He has supported them over the years simply because to a very high degree the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is socialist in concept.
However, Mr. Chairman, I want to comment on one or two things the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, and 1 do not want to comment in too harsh a fashion. I think there were some things left out, some things he did not say, that are perhaps as significant as those he did say.
He said he enjoyed most of the programs over the C.B.C. No one can criticize him for that. While I am not a radio fiend, one who sits at his radio day and night, and I do not own a television set, because there is not a television station within about 1,000 miles of my home-and I do not expect there will be for some little time-I must confess that I enjoy many of the programs that come over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation stations.
But the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spent considerable time applauding the C.B.C. for its televising of the coronation. I did not see it over television and I suppose they did a good job. I am quite willing to give them credit for that. I saw the coronation in the motion pictures and I too was very much impressed. But the thing my hon. friend did not say was that the televising of the coronation over the Canadian stations was merely a televising of the film. Well, now, there is no trick in televising a film. The trick is in producing the film in the first place. The good job I thought the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation did was the most important one of getting this film over here without any delay.

Supply-National Revenue
I think they are to be commended on that, for it was seen here practically within hours of the actual coronation taking place. It is nice to laud that program, but I would point out that that was not merely a feature of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Any TV station which had a similar film could have done the same job.
There are good programs on the C.B.C., and the work the C.B.C. is doing is commendable. This group has never criticized the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the way in which it is conducting its own affairs in respect to the programs that it puts on. What we have criticized is the government radio policy in Canada of permitting the C.B.C., which is a government institution, to be a monopoly.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, "Yes, but there are other monopolies," just as though one wrong justifies another. But that is not so. I do not know what control the government may have over commercial monopolies such as that mentioned by my hon. friend, but they certainly do have control over radio and television in Canada and they seem very determined to maintain that control as a monopoly. Just because there are other monopolies does not mean that this one should continue to exist.
We have not even criticized-not too harshly, at least-the method of financing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We have not vigorously opposed these expenditures. In our speeches we have said that we believe a good deal of the expenditure could be cut down. On numerous occasions we have said that if private radio stations were given the opportunity of carrying on a separate network and were given more latitude in the operation of radio and, in the future, of television, money could be saved. We have advocated and said-I personally have said it from time to time and I still believe it- that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, although government-owned, should be able to function on a commercial basis side by side with independent and private radio, and that if independent and private radio can "make a go of it" financially, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be able to do the same thing. But even though we have said that, we have been willing to subsidize them. We have been willing to subsidize them for those sustaining programs that do not bring in any revenue. I do not think that we could be any fairer than that.
We did not vigorously oppose the new policy introduced a little while ago, namely, that of doing away with the licence fees and the collection of the sales tax on radio and television equipment; we did not vigorously
Mr. HanselL]
oppose that policy. That is a nice handsome sum that is coming to the corporation over and above the commercial revenues which they receive and which would not be coming to private radio. Yet private radio could handle the job without that subsidy. As yet we have not vigorously opposed that procedure; we have not vigorously opposed subsidizing of the C.B.C. But what we have opposed-and I repeat it again-is the placing of the control of radio in the hands of the corporation which controls its competitors. That is the position we have taken, and I think that is the most sensible position that anyone could possibly take.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spoke in terms of independent radio control -I think that was the phrase he used-as though those of us who may be critics of the corporation were wanting to put the control of radio into private hands. We have never advocated that course. What we have advocated is that a separate regulatory body be set up. It could be easily set up by nominations coming to the government as to the personnel of such a body. I do not care whether it is called a commission or something else. The government could appoint one member; perhaps they could call upon the independent stations to appoint another; and perhaps those two could even appoint a third. Those are incidental details about which we are not greatly concerned. However, we are not advocating, as the hon. member hinted-I do not think that he perhaps did it intentionally; it may have been a slip of the tongue-that private radio should be the controlling force of radio in Canada. We have recommended that certain phases of radio and television should be controlled but have maintained that they should not be controlled by the government-owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
There is one other matter upon which I should like to say a few words. The speech of the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C., as it was given at the convocation of Saskatchewan University, has been brought into the picture. I did not hear the speech but I know the gentleman well enough to know that his speech would be carefully given. I would not think for a moment that Mr. Dunton would advocate a tightening up of the control of speech; I do not think he wants that. I can quite understand his advocating, in his speech, the greatest measure possible of freedom of speech; I quite suppose that he did that. But according to what I have read in the papers I believe that he may have made just a little slip. I am quoting from a newspaper article which reports that in the course of his speech he

said this-I might say that the article is from the Winnipeg Tribune and it reads as follows:
The C.B.C. chairman warned that there was a danger to the free and fair interchange of ideas when power over mass communication was "in the hands of so few".
He went on to say: "I am very conscious of this myself because I and others of the C.B.C. belong to the few, together with controllers of publishing, film and other broadcasting organizations".
The point of this newspaper editorial and the point I want to bring out is simply this. We can place the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the same category as that of other mediums of publication, as far as the principle of publication is concerned. I want to make that point clear. In my own mind the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is just as much a medium of publication as is any newspaper or any motion picture theatre. I put them all in the same category. I do not think there can be any denial of that statement. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation puts on plays and feature programs, so do the newspapers and so do the magazines of our country-the only difference is that in the one instance the vehicle is the spoken word and in the other it is the printed word. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation also put on newscasts, and they are to be complimented on the way in which they are given. The newspapers also publish news. That is what they were originally intended for. That is why they are called newspapers. The newspapers advertise in their columns. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation also advertise by reason of their commercially sponsored programs. Comparing them as mediums of publication, one can find no difference.
The one difference is this. The chairman of the board of governors linked himself with the publishers, producers of motion pictures and other radio station operators, and thus indicated that there was an association. Eecently we have heard a great deal about the imposition of guilt by association. I am not going to say that there is any guilt in this case. I think the opposite is the case so far as his speech is concerned. What he has determined is more or less a type of responsibility by reason of association, and that is all right. I am not criticizing that, but where the difference arises is that in the case of radio and television there is a monopoly of control. Anyone in this country who can raise the funds can institute a newspaper or publication house for the printing of literature if he wishes to do so without having to go to some higher national body for a licence. The same thing is true
Supply-National Revenue with respect to motion pictures. Anyone can take motion pictures. I have a motion picture camera myself. Anyone can go into the business if they want to and nobody is going to stop them.
There are many motion picture producing companies in Canada. I have a return in my office which I forgot to bring to the chamber that indicates there are many motion picture producing companies in Canada. I have forgotten how many there are, but anyone can start such a company if they want to do so. You do not have to have a licence unless it is a business licence in a city or community in which the company is established, and that is only a matter of routine.
The fact of the matter is that the difference between the various mediums of publication is that the C.B.C. controls its competitors while the other mediums of publication are free, and that is a very basic difference. In the past we in this party have advocated two things. We have advocated that the radio committee should be made a regular standing committee that would meet every year. I am not going to take any time now on that point. The other thing we have recommended, and I have mentioned it previously, is that there should be a separate regulatory body. We can talk how we like and try to pare down the view that the C.B.C. is not a monopoly, but it still remains a monopoly. It remains a monopoly in three spheres.
In the first place, to a very large extent it is a commercial monopoly. I want to be fair in analysing that particular point because it is not true to say that it has a complete monopoly of commercial broadcasting. The independent radio stations are getting along reasonably well financially, and I do not think that they are complaining too much about that. They are paid a nominal sum for carrying the commercial broadcasts that are sent out over the networks by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. But nevertheless there is a certain degree of monopoly in the commercial field, particularly in national network commercial programs.
I have been referring particularly to sound broadcasting, but we are now entering the field of television. It is still in its infant stage, and I must say that so far as licensing is concerned I think the field should be pretty well wide open so that private television interests can develop television in Canada wherever it is possible to obtain a channel in order that private industry may to a large extent bear the financial responsibility of the expansion that must take place

Supply-National Revenue within the next few years in this field. Otherwise we are going to have a monopoly of commercial television broadcasting in Canada. I am most sincere on that point.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out that in talking to one man he asked him if he expected to go into the television field and the man said that he did not know, that it would cost him a lot of money to get started, anywhere from $150,000 to $500,000. That may be so. I will not doubt that but that is all the more reason for giving the private television interests all the encouragement possible to go into the field. If it costs so much, then it is going to cost equally as much for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to cover the entire area of Canada.
While it may cost a good deal in the initial stages to engage in the operation of a television station, it can be a fairly good paying proposition. I do not know whether it is altogether accurate for me to compare Canadian figures with those of the United States, but I have an article in my hand from a magazine known as Tide to which I should like to refer. It is an old issue of three or four years ago. I am not going to read the article but it does give an account of a television station in a community with a population of 28,000 people. That is a small city. I think the population of the city of Lethbridge would be about 25,000.
New Westminster has 28,000.

The hon. member for New Westminster says that New Westminster has 28,000. But of course there is a difference because any television station in New Westminster would reach many more than 28,000 people. It would reach a population of well-nigh a million people in that area. But here is the community of Bloomington, Indiana- I might as well give the name-with a population of 28,000 people, and yet within two years the television station there was operating at a profit. As I say, I do not know whether it is completely fair for me to compare that with Canada, but I do not see why the figures should not be reasonably comparable.
I have been talking about monopoly in the commercial field. I should also like to say a word concerning monopoly in the cultural field. I believe we are going astray in our thinking when we say that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has responsibility for the cultural interests in the nation. In my opinion culture is something that you may aid through radio or TV. You may do that just as well, I suppose, as you can demoralize the life of the people by the same process. I realize that, but a lot of

these things, such as culture and the social complex of many things, originate very largely and are the responsibility of the home and other institutions.
I refer to this because it has been said often that the plowing of money into the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not lost by reason of the artists developed through their activities, the encouragement given to musicians and artists of one kind or another. I maintain this, and I think I am right, that talent is not produced by radio or TV, but talent is something that is inborn. Talent is something that is not trained; it is something that is discovered. I say it is a misconception to lean over backwards in our thinking or to be too much concerned with what the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is doing to develop a certain type of culture in Canada. If they do insist upon that, then I say that is all the more reason why TV and radio should have more opportunity. I do not believe you can discover or develop culture by going through one individual channel.
Who is to decide what type of culture we want in Canada? Culture comes from all directions. In Canada we are in a particularly favourable position in that respect. We are a people of various racial origins bringing our various cultures from various parts of the world. If those cultures could be brought together in some way or other, we could produce a tremendous Canadian culture that would be comparable with any in the world. But it should be free; it should be open. All the airways and the TV channels should be open to the entire country and the material should not be all put through one particular channel.
Then I come to what is most important of all. I have not kept my eye on the clock, and I do not want to go over my time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps I should have advised the hon. member that his time had expired, but I presume the committee has been giving unanimous consent to the hon. member continuing.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman; I appreciate that. I shall only be a minute or two, otherwise I would have to rise a litle later. I come now to the very serious principle of thought control. I know there are many officials in radio, particularly in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, who are willing to say, "We do not want to channel the thinking of Canada through only one medium." I believe they are honourable men. Nevertheless, the principle is there, and all the apparatus is there; the organization is there. If you have control of the one

medium in Canada that controls all radio and TV throughout the country, then of necessity you cannot escape being charged with monopoly of thought control. There is only one channel of thought control. That is a monopoly more vicious than any other control to be found anywhere, and much more vicious than the monopolies mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Perhaps the International Nickel Company is a monopoly, but what can nickel do? It is only a piece of metal. I do not believe that nickel has any brains.
Thought control.

The hon. member says
"thought control". I cannot see any brains or the ability of nickel to think.
Is that a reflection on an hon. member?
If he is a nickel-headed member, I suppose it is.
What about their ads?

The hon. member refers to their ads, but that is a different medium altogether. It is the realm of publication again. This thought control is a serious thing because if there is one thing the dictatorships of the earth want, it is thought control. Here is the medium through which that very thing is done. I do not think I could do any better than to quote from a radio broadcast that was given by Chester A. Bloom. The pamphlet copy I have is entitled "The Threat of Thought Control". I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if I might read just one paragraph from it? It is enlightening. I quote:
The real truth is that steady refusal to grant such fair rights can only be motivated by determination to maintain control over the thinking of the people of Canada. The government and the CBC are obviously determined to maintain the same kind of control over the public mind by means of television.
Let me give you just one small example of how this works. The talk I am making to you today will be broadcast from 67 independent radio stations in Canada. If I were giving it over the CBC network, as I often have, it would go out simultaneously and at an immediate hour. But because it is to be given by independent stations served by an independent bureau, it had to be copied on 67 records and mailed out separately to each station. That means a long delay before it can go on the air. Obviously, it also means that no such broadcast can deal with immediate events. This is a subtle handicap on freedom of speech over the radio.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I quote that because I think it is pertinent to the discussion. I shall conclude by amplifying that quotation by saying this: No individual in Canada could broadcast to this nation over a national network unless he received permission or was invited to do so by the small committee of 83276-350

It does not make any difference what kind of message he has; it does not make any difference what kind of proposals he has to make; it does not make any difference whether he has a million dollars, he could not do it without first receiving the sanction of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would you want the man with the million dollars to have the right to buy that time?
I know what my hon. friend means. He means that only those with money would be able to do it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You would have such persons controlling our thoughts.

Well, if all the money was in the hands of one person or one corporation, I would say that is so. The same thing applies to the newspaper business, the publication business. It takes millions of dollars for a man to float a daily newspaper; but you can do that anywhere in Canada, if you have the money. Does my hon. friend object to that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is my hon. friend satisfied with the treatment the press gives to members of parliament?
Well, I don't know that I am but, believe me, my hon. friend should be.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We thrive on the treatment they give us.

Yes, you surely do. And even though that may be the case, I would give the press the absolute right to function as they do today, with the privilege given to any person or any organization to be able to float a newspaper and to have a representative here in the press gallery.
May I ask a question?
Oh, for goodness' sake, he is ten minutes overtime now.
Does the statement by the hon. member for Macleod mean that he is repudiating the policy that the Alberta government followed in the press law a few years ago?
Now, Mr. Chairman, I don't know if you are going to permit me to answer that or not. I want to answer it. Because, Mr. Chairman, that very question has been asked over and over again.
And never answered.

And answered a good many times. Believe me, I have not been floating around from coast to coast in this country

Supply-National Revenue without having that question popped at me a good many times. I have not read the papers of this country without having that bit of propaganda put to me a good many times-and also misrepresented, as is the intention of my hon. friend's question. Yes, I will explain.
I prefer the view of the supreme court in the matter.

The supreme court's view
was that it was unconstitutional for that government to put it in; that was their view. What the press act did was this, that when a falsehood was given out in a news report of government activity, then the government had the right to correct that report.
Oh, oh.

If that is not thought
control, what is?

I am only answering the
question I was asked. The government should know what is the truth concerning its own actions. Let me ask the minister, who is a responsible minister of the crown, this question:	Does he know the truth? When
anything is reported about his department does he know the truth of that report?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If he knew the truth it would make him free from the Liberal party.
My respect for other people prompts me to say that I believe what they tell me, and that they do not tell me anything else but the truth.
Well, Mr. Chairman, the profundity of the minister's answer leaves me staggered and spellbound.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the time for levity has passed, and that we had better get back on the rail and discuss the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I will be glad to accommodate the minister. But let him not accuse me of getting off the track; it was my friend the Secretary of State who initiated it.
Now, I am against thought control.
Oh, oh.

And I believe every member in this house is. I believe those who are enjoying a little humour at the moment, if one may judge by their laughter, are also opposed to thought control. And, even to say the worst, even though I did not agree with the Alberta press act, if it is thought control then I would be against it. But I do not believe it is.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with its control over sound radio and television, is the only medium through which there can be freedom of expression over networks in Canada. That is what I am opposed to. I will always oppose it. While I am reasonable in wanting the broadcasting corporation to stay out of the red, and while I am willing to cast my vote for appropriations wherever they are needed, while I commend them on the work they are doing, I must seriously and vigorously criticize government radio and television policy for its monopolistic principles.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to attempt to answer the opinions expressed by the hon. member of the opposite side as the hon. minister can ably do it. First of all, I should like to commend the C.B.C. upon the effort it has made in trying to give to the Ottawa area television programs which would satisfy both elements in the community. I believe however that they have not succeeded in this. I may be told that this is neither the time nor the place to discuss this subject, and it may be pointed out to me that permits are issued by the Department of Transport. However, those permits are given out or are refused in accordance with the policy laid down by the Department of National Revenue.

Not knowing exactly where to go I have taken advantage of the opportunity afforded this afternoon to ask the minister if anything can be done to meet the situation I shall describe. As I said before, the broadcasting corporation has made a noteworthy effort. But, under present circumstances, a large proportion of the English-speaking population of this area do not speak French, and it will be kept in mind that a considerable part of the programming is in French. Then, there is a proportion of the French-speaking population who do not speak English, and, again, hon. members will realize that a considerable portion of the television is in English.
As it is, neither the French-speaking nor the English-speaking portions of the population are fully satisfied. While the programs may be satisfactory in both languages, they do not satisfy those elements for which the television system has been established.
I know an attempt was made by station CKCH to establish another channel. This may not have come before the Minister of National Revenue. However I have spoken about it to the Minister of Transport and found that he was not opposed to the idea. But they are governed by the regulations which say that two television systems cannot be installed within a radius of fifty miles or so. I can understand that perfectly if the same broadcasts were coming from Toronto or Montreal over the French or English system; that is, if there were two of those systems in the same vicinity it would be too many. In Montreal they established a French system and also an English system, because there was a large element that was in need of that service. We have the very same situation in Hull and Ottawa. the second reading of Bill No. 390, to amend the Canada Elections Act (age of voters).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe that in a democracy we should have the widest possible basis for our franchise. Over the years progress has been made in broadening the basis for eligibility of voters. Gradually property qualifications have been abolished, voting has been extended to women and now every Canadian subject is allowed to vote on reaching the age of 21. But I believe there is just one group remaining in the country that should be given the franchise, and that is the group from 18 years of age to 21. I believe that that group should be given the vote, because if one looks over their education, qualifications, and their knowledge I think it will be seen that that group is the best educated group in Canada. I believe that their knowledge on public affairs is second to that of no other age group in the nation.
Over the years our educational standards have been going up. People have been leaving school at a more advanced age. In 1911 the average 18-year old had a grade VII education. Thirty years later the average 18-year-old had a grade X education. The

1951 census showed once again that the educational standards of the Canadian people are rising, and that the average Canadian had been in school -5 years longer in 1951 than when the previous census was taken in 1941.
At present a person is eligible to vote when he or she becomes 21, provided, of course, there is a general election at that time. We usually have a federal general election every four or five years, so that the average Canadian, in practice, is not able to cast his first ballot until he is 22 or 23 years of age. If we lowered the age of voters to 18 you would not give every person in Canada of 18 years of age a vote in a federal election at 18. That would depend on when the federal general election was called. It would mean that the average citizen would vote for the first time at the average age of 19 or 20, rather than 22 or 23 which is the practical result of having the vote at the age of 21.
I believe that a student coming out of high school should be able to vote as soon thereafter as possible, as far as age qualification is concerned. I do not think it lends itself to young Canadians keeping and maintaining an interest in public affairs to have a long gap of years between the time they graduate from high school and the time they are eligible to vote. I believe young Canadians would take a more active interest in public affairs if the voting age were lowered to 18.
We know that from our own experience in Saskatchewan. You can go out to Saskatchewan and you can campaign in a federal election, and you will find that your audience is older on the average than when you campaign in that province during a provincial election, because in Saskatchewan we have given our citizens the right to vote at the age of 18. Campaigning in a provincial election you find a substantial proportion of your audience are teen-agers, and I can tell you that they do take an active interest in public affairs; they do take their right to vote seriously; and they do attend public meetings. I think if they are encouraged in that way, by reducing the voting age, to attend political meetings at an early age that that interest is more likely to continue in the years ahead.
Saskatchewan is not the only province in Canada which has reduced its voting age. In 1944 Alberta reduced the voting age in the province to 19; in 1953 British Columbia reduced its voting age to 19. Saskatchewan, however, is the first and only province in Canada so far to reduce the voting age to 18. I believe that young Canadians between the ages cf 18 and 21, no matter what other
Canada Elections Act
hon. members in this house may think and say, are responsible persons, and I think they are sufficiently responsible to be given the right to vote, and to be given the right to have a voice in public affairs.
Whenever the country faces an emergency, whenever the country is engaged in war, then we are quite happy to extend the voting principle to 18-year olds when they are in the armed forces. If we are prepared to do that when we need them to defend democracy in wartime, why should they be denied the right to vote in peacetime, the right to a voice in public affairs, and the right to a voice by the ballot in the decisions that will be made which may result in their having to don a uniform and lay down their lives for their country.
Canada was prepared to spend huge sums of money in giving a very intricate and thorough training to young Canadians during the war. They showed themselves capable of undertaking that training by assimilating knowledge, and they were able to operate very efficiently the most intricate and complicated instruments of war. Of this I am sure: Some day the 18-year-olds in Canada will have the franchise. It is just a matter of time. The trend is already apparent. Three of the ten provinces in Canada have reduced the voting age. Of another thing we can be sure, when the C.C.F. party becomes the government in any other province, the voting age will be reduced to 18. From two precedents I think it also follows that should the Social Credit party be elected in any other province in Canada, the chances are that the voting age in that province will be reduced to 19. Hence the trend is definitely for a reduction in the voting age. I am sure the age will be reduced to 18. It is only a matter of time; and I do not see why the time should not be now.
President Eisenhower of the United States is himself in favour of giving the vote to young Americans 18 years of age. He presented that proposal to congress in his speech on January 7 in these words:
For years our citizens between the ages of 18 and 21 have, in time of peril, been summoned to fight for America. They should participate in the political process that produces this fateful summons. I urge congress to propose to the states a constitutional amendment permitting citizens to vote when they reach the age of 18.
Gerald Waring points out in his column that at least one section of another political party in Canada other than the C.C.F. is in favour of giving the franchise to 18-year-olds. In his column on May 6 he states as follows:
Last month the provincial Liberal convention in Ontario joined the national C.C.F. party in favouring a reduction of the voting age minimum to 18 years.

They did not join the national C.C.F. party; they merely favoured the granting of the franchise at 18.

If the hon. member wants to quarrel with the way in which Gerald Waring wrote his column, that is all right; but to me it is perfectly clear that what he is saying is that the Ontario Liberal convention joined the C.C.F. party in favouring a reduction of the voting age to 18 years.

I am sure the hon. member would not wish to mislead anyone by his remarks; I am quite sure of that. I was merely pointing out that what the young Liberals did was to recommend that the franchise be granted at age 18. They did not join the C.C.F. party.
I am sure there is no move on foot by the C.C.F. to have the Ontario Liberal party join the national C.C.F. I am sure of that. We do not want the kiss of death now or at any other time.
You have had it.

After President Eisenhower had called on congress to lower the voting age to 18, the matter was discussed in the United States senate. The proposition that the voting age should be reduced to 18 was passed in the United States senate by a vote of 34 to 24. In other words, the senators in the United States, by a substantial majority, are in favour of a reduction in the voting age to 18. That vote cannot result in the enactment of the necessary constitutional amendment because, in order to have such a constitutional amendment such a proposition must have a two-thirds majority. In this particular vote, the majority came close to but did not quite reach the necessary two-thirds.
I think the President of the United States is proposing something that is reasonable, sensible and progressive and something that the United States will adopt in time. Certainly the vote in the United States senate shows that a substantial part of congress is in favour of reducing the voting age. I hope that our government here will consider a reduction in the voting age and will bring in-if not during this present session, at least before the next general election-the necessary legislation to bring about this result. I naturally hope that the bill I am presenting will get the support of the majority of hon. members. However, if that support should not be forthcoming I am hoping that the government itself, before the next general election, will bring in legislation to provide for a reduction of the voting age to 18.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say a few words on this bill. It is not the first time that this bill or a similar one has come before the house, but I did not avail myself of addressing the house on previous occasions. Before going further I naturally want to state that I agree fully with the first part of what the hon. member had to say. I am sure we all agree that universal suffrage is the goal today, in theory and in practice, of most governments throughout the world at the present time. However, even though that is the situation, we must all recognize the fact that there are certain inhabitants of states that cannot be given the right to vote. In this country and in most other democracies the only ones excluded are the insane and the minors.
And judges.

In considering this bill the questions arise as to who is a minor and when a person ceases to be a minor. I realize that the tendency in this country-and indeed in many others-is to lower the voting age from 21 to 18. The age varies a great deal, even right in Canada. Various provinces have taken various ages, all the way from 18 to 21, but I believe there are several countries in the world where the age is still 25. This great hurry to get the people to vote no doubt flows from what I often think is our great hurry to get our children educated in this country. I sometimes wonder whether we are not nowadays trying to rush our education a little bit too much. In days gone by children would start to school at the age of 7; then they started to go to school at 6. Now they start at the age of 5, and even at the age of 4. There is a tendency to try to rush them through as soon as possible and to get them out into life as soon as possible.
I am quite satisfied that the average young man and the average young woman at the age of 17 in this country is quite responsible enough to exercise, and quite capable of exercising, his or her franchise in this country. However, the point that comes to my mind is this: Are we wise or are we fair in imposing upon them the responsibility of being obliged to cast a vote at that age? It is true that it is a great privilege to exercise the franchise in a country. But something more than a privilege is involved. Great responsibility is entailed in the exercise of this right of the franchise.
For one thing it would seem to me that to lower the age at the federal level would be premature in Canada at this stage. I must say quite frankly that I think the hon. member would have a hard time justifying 18

more than 19 or 19 more than 18 or even 17 more than 18. I admit it is very hard to draw the line, and the line has to be drawn more or less in an arbitrary way. Up until now the line has been drawn at age 21.
I do not think there are any very great reasons to justify lowering that age by even one year. I might at some time agree that there might be some justification for lowering it by one year or two years, but I frankly wonder whether it would be a service, as the hon. member has just said, to this class. Here again I do not know why he classes those from 18 to 21 in a special group. I wonder whether it would really be a favour to them to impose the responsibility on them of casting their vote.
Surely there does not seem to be any very keen desire on their part to exercise their responsibility at the present time. Taking the results of the last election, if they were to follow the example set by their elders, that would seem to be an indication that there is not a very keen desire on the part of any particular group to go to the polls on voting day. According to the results of the last election, even the older people did not go to the polls in the numbers that they should have. There is no doubt that even in the group from 18 to 21 the same attitude probably prevails. That is just incidental, but I thought I would mention it.
Even today when our children go to school at an early age and are rushed through as quickly as possible it is my experience that the average person at age 18, if he is going to take up a profession, is still in the process of getting his professional education, and he has not yet taken over the actual responsibilities of life or become interested in the intricacies and application of government. I think it is also true of the average high school student who, as the hon. member has said, may attend meetings, will still have fresh in his memory the knowledge of what government is and how it is constituted. They have the theory of government fresh in their minds but they have not yet had to deal with the application of the theory.
Mind you, there are a certain number who by the age of 18 are already established in life, but they would be a minority. The greater number of those from 18 to 21 are quite busy at that stage in deciding on their future. They have a very great decision to make. They have to decide how they will grapple with life in the years to come. For the most part their minds are quite preoccupied and they have little time for the actual application of politics in the country.

I would question whether there is actually a long gap, as the hon. member said, from the time they leave school and become established in life and the time they actually cast their first vote. I would think in most cases the gap might be a year or two or three years at the most.
The point I should like to come back to is that these people will have plenty of opportunity to discharge the responsibility of voting in the years to come. I think it is not a bad principle to give them a chance to establish themselves and to become accustomed to their environment after assuming the full responsibilities of citizenship and all that goes with it. Then they are automatically and, generally speaking, naturally ready to assume the responsibility of the franchise.
Whether there is any great merit in having them break in gradually, so to speak, so far as voting is concerned is a very debatable question and one that could be debated for a long time. Inasmuch as some provinces have a lower voting age it would seem to me that the first step would be to give this group the vote first at the lower levels of government. I do not think it would be logical to have students or young people voting in federal elections when they did not have the right to vote in provincial or municipal elections. It seems to me they should be given the privilege first at the lower level. Once they have been granted the responsibility of the franchise at a lower age at the provincial level generally throughout the country, then in my opinion that would be the time to consider giving them the same responsibility on the federal level.
But it seems to me it would not be quite logical for them to start to vote in federal elections before they could vote at the lower levels. As far as I can ascertain at the moment, there is no great desire on the part of this group to cast their votes at that early age. I remember reading an article a few weeks ago in one of the local papers at home. In passing, I might say that it is a progressive and well illustrated weekly. I refer to the Carillon News. From time to time that paper makes it a practice to take a crosssection of public opinion and question people generally on various questions that arise.
A few weeks ago they questioned a crosssection of the high school students at the college and asked them if they were in favour of voting at the age of 19. I suppose they picked the age of 19 because the last provincial government that dealt with the question set that as the age. However, the response from the high school students was

Canada Elections Act
very much divided. A great many held that they would rather wait a few more years until they were established. Some thought that they were quite qualified and quite ready to assume the responsibility. A week later the newspaper asked the same question of a group of senior citizens, and again opinion was very much divided. No clear-cut pattern was apparent in the minds of these two classes of citizens. Therefore I say that there is no great demand for such a move at the present time. If the age is to be lowered I would, as I say, much prefer to see it done first at the lower levels of government before it is done at the federal level.
I am not questioning whether the young people are responsible or qualified at that age. I am quite convinced that they are fully qualified and capable of casting an intelligent vote at that age. The question that I have in mind is whether these heavy responsibilities should be placed on their shoulders at that early age. Why not give them a little break until the age of 21 when they would have an even better working knowledge of the intricacies of life and the intricacies of the various levels of government.

This bill, when it is passed, will make it possible for Canadian voters to exercise their franchise in federal elections when they reach the age of 18 years. At this time I wish to compliment the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) for sponsoring this bill and for the interest he is taking in the youth of this country. I believe that he is an example of what the young people of Canada can do when they get an early start and are interested in public affairs. At the age of 24 he was sitting as a member of this house, and is an example of what can be done by the youth of this country. He became interested in public affairs at an early age in the university parliament in the University of Saskatchewan. His interest in the future citizens of Canada and his faith in the ability of the young people of this country I am sure to a large extent have motivated him in sponsoring this bill and urging the young people to take a greater part in the affairs of Canada.
Some members in this house have opposed this bill on the grounds that young Canadians are too immature; that they are not interested in the affairs of state. If that is so, I feel it is a sad commentary on the educational standards of this country. One of the contributing causes of that lack of interest, if there is that lack, may lie in the very fact that they are not permitted to participate in these activities. They feel excluded. Do

hon. members realize that in spite of the fact the qualifying age of voters is now 21 the young people of Canada who reached their 21st birthday on August 10 last will not exercise their franchise in the ordinary course of events until they are 24 or 25 years of age. If this bill were passed and the minimum age were set at 18, still the average age of a Canadian casting his first vote would be about 20. I maintain that at that age young Canadians are capable of exercising their franchise in a very real way.
If any precedent is necessary I would refer the members of this house to the record of the first provincial government in Canada to grant the right to vote to those who are 18. That province has taken the lead in social legislation, and improving within its own jurisdiction the conditions of the people. It is now one of the most progressive provinces in the whole Dominion of Canada. I can remember sitting in this house when a young man from that province sat here as the member for Weyburn. He was elected when about 31, and at the age of 41 he became the premier of Saskatchewan. He is now making a signal contribution to Canadian history in the form of progressive legislation. That government is really working for the people, in the interests of the people and is in truth governed by the people.
In that province we urge the young people to participate and to feel that they are a part of this Canada. We urge them that part of their responsibilities as citizens of Canada is to take part in the elections of that province. It has been my privilege to live in that province for over 50 years. I have watched the youth grow. I know something about them and their attitude towards public affairs today. They are capable and they are responsible. When Canada finds herself in the position when she must defend her shores and the democratic rights of government, there are no members in this house who say the young people lack ability; that they lack skill or that they are not responsible or mature. The records indicate that the youths of 18, 19 and 20 take on the responsibilities of men much senior to that, and exercise a judgment and skill that has placed Canada high in the records of those who fight for democratic rights.
Surely those rights should be granted in time of peace to these same people when they reach that age. If they are fit to go out and die for their country, surely they are fit to vote for the policies for that country. It is a well established fact that we learn by doing. How could we do better than to encourage the young people at the age when they learn easily to take part in government? This will

urge people to learn more about their government, learn more about the policies of government and learn more about the effect of government upon the history of their own nation. Surely that could be only for the good of any country. Surely the knowledge of the masses is the one thing that democracy needs. Only those who are the enemies of democracy would deny or talk against knowledge for the masses. The passage of this bill will be a move to encourage the youth of Canada to take an active part in the democratic processes by an early exercise of their right to vote. They will be ready to study the problems of the country and the means of solving them. Youth, when it is urged by proper motives, can achieve miracles.
I watched a young man who could not find his place in the classroom of an ordinary high school. He left high school and entered the air force. Suddenly he became imbued with the idea that he wanted to have the wings of the Royal Air Force pinned upon his chest. He could overcome almost any obstacle. He could study and master the necessary sciences. He passed and stood there proudly as the wing commander placed these wings upon his breast. This made a man of him. He did not know what he could do, his parents did not know his abilities, until he became inspired by a desire to achieve something. Let us support this bill as a measure which will inspire the youth of this country to make Canada the greatest contributor to human progress in the world.

I am
going to make a very sort contribution to this debate, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I may be excused for making it rather personal. I have just been trying, as well as I can, to look back on my own life and try to assess myself as a voter between the years of 18 and 21. The result is not satisfactory.

There is a very obvious answer to that, I know, and anyone who wishes to make it can make it. I can only speak for myself.
I want to come to another point that has been referred to already, and that is the disappointing sense of responsibility that is shown even by those who have the vote, as judged by the performance at the last election.
The point I want to make is this. I have been reading an interesting book on the progress of civilization. It does not make one feel too happy because the whole purport of it is to show how civilization is becoming more and more a mass affair in which it is

harder and harder to preserve individuality, and those qualities which I think civilization had more obviously fifty years ago than it has today. The same writer points out that on this continent progress toward mass civilization is growing faster than anywhere else. Partly for reasons given by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), I find myself with the feeling that what we need is not to add to the mass; what we need to do is to try to give people more time. Mr. Speaker, I am sorry this measure has come up in the way it has. When I say that I am referring particularly to the attitude of the sponsor of the bill when he seeks to make it a party measure, and has introduced for its support a line of provincial politics which has nothing to do with the issue or the subject matter. And he seemed to be supported rather strongly in that by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden).
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that there was nothing in my address which would lead to that conclusion, at all.
Oh, oh.
I merely pointed out an example of where it was being used.

In support of what I have said I would refer to the hon. member's remarks about the premier of one of our provinces, and the government of that province. This is a subject which has been of great interest to me for many years, and I had hoped that it would not be treated as the hon. member has treated it. With due deference, provincial governments have their own responsibilities and tasks and I, for one, object to having them dragged in here, and their merits or demerits constantly talked about. I regret that the hon. member saw fit to take this opportunity to drag it in, in a left-handed way, and then lay on the praise

Canada Elections Act
for their operations. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss their merits or demerits, but it seems to me this is not the proper place to do it. The hon. member for Yorkton, of course, may have his views in the matter.
There is one other point that should be pointed out concerning the hon. member's speech. He made some comments about members of the armed forces that would have the support of all of us, but at no time in his speech did he admit that the armed forces already have the vote. On the other hand the sponsor of the bill was very clear on the point, and did make it clear in his remarks. The hon. member for Yorkton did not.
If one wanted to go into the background of this subject he would find that the party on this side of the house is the one that has carried the historic battle for the extension of the franchise. But, be that as it may, the situation in which we now find ourselves is one which I believe the whole population in Canada has pretty well accepted and agreed to the proposition that we should have the widest possible base among our citizens for eligibility to vote. I believe that is common ground among all parties.
The problem confronting those who concern themselves with the age limit in the elections act is that of deciding when a person has assumed the responsibilities of citizenship. And that is a difficult problem. It is not simply a matter of saying that at this age or at that age they assume those responsibilities. The law in most of its aspects gives them full responsibility at the age of 21. Generally speaking, the armed forces take them in at the age of 18 and, in some branches I believe, at 17J. In some parts of the services it may be younger than that. Where it is clear that citizens as members of the armed forces have assumed the responsibilities of citizenship in the highest way, immediately they are given the vote.
What we have to determine here is at what point a citizen not in the armed forces assumes full responsibility. Where is the line? About all one can do in the elections act is to choose an arbitrary age, and no matter what that age is, whether it be 21, 19, 18, 17 or at some other point, it is going to be possible to argue, and with real weight and authority, that there are some under that age who have assumed a very high degree of responsibility in the community. On the other hand it will also be possible to argue that there are some above the age who have not yet come to the full responsibilities of citizenship.

The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has referred to teen-agers attending election meetings. I would tell him that last summer I saw a great number of teenagers under the age of 18 years who attended open-air election meetings. Following the hon. member's argument, those persons should have the right to vote. Let me say seriously that the training the young people have under our school system is indeed extraordinary in this respect. They have good information and a considerable amount of knowledge about public affairs. I mention this only to show that it cannot be argued that simply because a person under 21 years attends an election meeting he should be allowed to vote.
This question has been discussed at parliamentary committees which in the past have studied the elections act. The suggested change has been turned down. I, for one, have felt that while in the circumstances what was done was wholly proper, the treatment given the subject in those committees was scarcely adequate. To treat this subject adequately it seems that one would have to examine the whole question. One would have to look into our legislation which gives added income tax exemption for educational purposes in respect of those over 16 years. Deduction allowances for children for income tax purposes normally stop at the age of 16.
We have what I regard, and I believe is also regarded by members of all parties, as a very fine provision permitting the extension of that exemption beyond the age of 16 when they are continuing their education. I do not want at this late date in the session when there is an attempt to amend the elections act in an arbitrary fashion to do something which would be quoted against me later when we come to extend some of the educational provisions about which I am rather partial. When I refer to that subject I am, of course, also including the subject of scholarships. I am not going to digress into that educational field, but I think we have made good progress in the last few years, and I hope we can go further in developing provisions for the education of the young people.
A nice question arises when one has to decide at just what age a young person who is wholly maintained by his parents should receive the right to vote. Certainly he is not in the same position as his fellow classmate who enlisted in the armed services and is on active service. It is that type of question I would like to see examined and discussed more fully.
As I said in opening my remarks, this is a subject that has absorbed my attention to

a considerable degree in the past. It is something that should be examined into pretty thoroughly, but I should like it to come up in another way so that we could really look at these things. I should like to get some more statistical information on one or two aspects of it. The hon. member who is sponsoring the bill-I am not critical of him-is naturally enthusiastic about it. He said that if we do not get it now we shall get it later. That is not the issue to be determined here. The issue before the house is an amendment to the elections act. Incidentally, I think there is a technical mistake in the bill about the armed forces. Be that as it may, that is the issue before the house. I do not think that issue should be determined in that way at all now.
It may be that the age should be reduced. I am certainly openminded, and rather inclined to think that probably it should be reduced; but I am not prepared to amend the elections act at this time on a few speeches to reduce the age from 21 to 18 without further consideration and without a full examination of what I consider to be the real facets that must be considered before a decision is taken. I realize that that may not be acceptable to the hon. member proposing the bill, but I think it is the right way to go about it. I for one do not wish to see something done here in a rush to amend the elections act that is going to hamper things that I hope we can do in the next few years by way of extending the opportunity for education through scholarships and educational grants. I do not want anything done here rashly that is going to interfere with that. I should like therefore to have this matter considered in what-if I may use the term and not be misunderstood-I believe to be a more mature way. I am in favour of the idea behind the suggestion, but I think this method of dealing with the subject is at least premature.
Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I do want to deal with one statement, because sometimes these repeated statements made in a certain recurring confusion of the mind become embedded in the minds of others. I do want to deal with this very briefly because we so constantly hear statements about the great achievements of the party opposite in every field-
Hear, hear.
-no matter what it may be.
Right.

Once in a while it may do some of them good to be reminded of the fact that this has become a habit that leads them to make those statements without any regard to the actual history of the country. The fact is that the voting age and the general principles in regard to voting were established under a Conservative party which had the responsibility of setting up the electoral machinery in this country in the first instance. There were a number of extensions during the life of that continuing Conservative government, and then the next great step in the extension of the franchise came in 1918 when Sir Robert Borden was head of the government. In May 1918, the franchise was extended to all women of the age of 21, and there you had universal franchise subject only to the age limit. With deference to the admiration that the hon. member who has just spoken constantly expresses for the history of his own party, I would suggest that from time to time it might be well to restrain that enthusiasm within the bounds of the actual political history of this country.
There is one aspect of this problem that I do think should be borne in mind by all hon. members. I do not think there is any single member here on either side of the house who is not equally proud of the type of young people of 18 to 21 that we have here in Canada. Our education, the type of life in a country of wide spaces and immense opportunities has given us youth of whom all of us have every reason to be proud. I am certain that neither one side of the house nor the other, nor in any segment of this house, is there any greater appreciation of the high character of our youth which would differentiate any hon. member from another. We all share that pride and we all have reason to share that pride. I do not want to sound offensive, but I do say very often that there are differences, and without being offensive I will say quite frankly that my youngest child, who is now fourteen, gives

evidence of judgment which I would be quite prepared to accept as against the judgment of a number who have spoken here.

Six o'clock.

If I may finish this sentence, there is just one point that should be given consideration in discussing this subject, namely, that the age of 21 was not chosen as an arbitrary age at which the ability to make a political decision had been reached; but it is the age at which for not only generations but centuries we have imposed upon young people a full legal liability. Until they are 21 we have provided that people up to that age need not be answerable for the contracts that are signed and other things of that kind, under the theory that their judgment may not be developed to the point that the full legal responsibility should be imposed.
The time may have come to change that concept in regard to that matter. The fact remains, however, that the choice of the voting age of 21 was not an arbitrary decision in regard to their political wisdom, but was related to the age of political responsibility. I would be the first to be ready to consider a change of the age, with my admiration of Canadian youth; but let us remember that this was the basis upon which the age was originally fixed, and we have to consider this when we are dealing with an ordinary change in voting age that is before us.
